## Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to <term>digitize<note>The process of converting physical text or images into a digital format.</note></term> public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive, so in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including placing technical restrictions on automated querying.

We also ask that you:

+ *Make non-commercial use of the files* We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.
+ *Refrain from automated querying* Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google’s system: If you are conducting research on machine translation, <term>optical character recognition<note>Often abbreviated as OCR; the electronic conversion of images of typed, handwritten or printed text into machine-encoded text.</note></term> or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.
+ *Maintain attribution* The Google “watermark” you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.
+ *Keep it legal* Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still in copyright varies from country to country, and we can’t offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book’s appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. Copyright infringement liability can be quite severe.

# ADVERTISEMENT. <note>In 19th-century publishing, an "Advertisement" usually refers to a preface or an introductory note by the editor or publisher explaining the purpose of the new edition.</note>

---

**THE** various translations and original works of Thomas Taylor, though still in request by the more zealous students of ancient philosophy and <term>occult science</term> <note>In this context, "occult science" refers to esoteric or "hidden" knowledge, specifically the spiritual and philosophical mysteries of the Neoplatonists, rather than modern magic.</note>, have now become so scarce and expensive that it is only within the power of comparatively wealthy collectors to obtain them. This is a matter for regret, inasmuch as it cannot be affirmed that his writings have been, or are likely to be superseded, or that they are without value. They can hardly be neglected without loss by those who desire to understand the systems of philosophy which satisfied the spiritual needs of the antique world. It is not possible, even for the most fervent believer in modern “progress,” to dismiss the speculations of the ancient philosophers as antiquated notions which have had their day and no longer possess interest or value. The names of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle can never grow dim with age, nor is it possible to conceive a time when men shall cease to study and reverence them. As the disciple, the translator, and the expounder of

<meta>This page concludes the publisher's preface (the "Advertisement") from the previous page and begins the title page of the 1895 edition. It explains the motivation for reprinting Thomas Taylor’s 19th-century translation of Iamblichus.</meta>

these and of other sages of antiquity, Thomas Taylor <note>Thomas Taylor (1758–1835) was an English scholar known as "the Platonist." He was the first to translate the complete works of Plato and Aristotle into English and was a key figure in the revival of ancient philosophy in the Romantic era.</note> deserves to be held in honour and remembrance, and it would be a misfortune if his labours remained unknown because of the scarcity of his books. It is for this reason that the present reprint has been undertaken; and it is hoped that it will meet with such a measure of success as may encourage the re-publication of various other works by the same author. It has been printed in handsome style and published at a moderate price in order that it may be regarded as a desirable addition to the scholar's library, while yet it will not tax severely the means of the not too wealthy student. For the rest it is only necessary to say that this reprint is, in size, number of pages, type, and general get-up, an almost exact <term>facsimile</term> <note>A "facsimile" is an exact reproduction or copy of an original printed work, preserving the original layout, typography, and pagination.</note> of the original edition, which was first printed in 1821. No alterations or additions have been made in or to the original text, as it is thought that those who care for Taylor's writings will prefer to have them in their integrity. Should it be found possible, however, to continue the series it is intended to prefix to a future volume an essay on Taylor, which will contain a biography of him, and a critical estimate of his writings.

*May, 1895.*

# INTRODUCTION.

---

It appears to me that there are two descriptions of persons <note>In this context, "descriptions of persons" refers to "types" or "categories" of people.</note> by whom the present work must be considered to be of inestimable worth: the lovers of antiquity and the lovers of ancient philosophy and religion. To the former of these it must be invaluable, because it is replete with information derived from the wise men of the **Chaldeans** <note>The Chaldeans were an ancient people of Mesopotamia (modern-day Iraq) famous in antiquity for their knowledge of astronomy and occult sciences.</note>, the prophets of the **Egyptians**, the dogmas <note>Here, "dogmas" refers to established theological teachings or philosophical principles rather than rigid or narrow-minded beliefs.</note> of the **Assyrians** <note>An ancient Near Eastern civilization; the author suggests their religious traditions influenced this work.</note>, and the ancient pillars of **Hermes** <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure said to have authored sacred texts on alchemy, magic, and philosophy.</note>; and to the latter, because of the doctrines contained in it, some of which originated from the **Hermaic pillars** <note>Legendary stone pillars inscribed with the secret wisdom and laws of ancient Egypt, attributed to the god Thoth (Hermes).</note>, were known by **Pythagoras** and **Plato** <note>Two of the most influential Greek philosophers; Pythagoras (6th century BC) is known for his mathematical and mystical teachings, and Plato (4th century BC) for his foundational works on metaphysics and ethics.</note>, and were the sources of their philosophy; and others are profoundly theological, and unfold the mysteries of ancient religion with an admirable conciseness of diction, and an inimitable vigour and elegance of conception. To

<meta>This page continues the introduction, moving from the historical origins of the text to a defense of its theological system and a summary of its core metaphysical principles. <page-num>viii</page-num>

To this we may add, as the crowning achievement <note>The original uses "colophon of excellence," referring to the finishing stroke or peak of quality.</note>, that this work is the most extensive, the clearest, and the most satisfying defense still in existence of true ancient theology.

This theology—the sacred rituals of which are called <term>theurgy</term> <note>From the Greek *theourgia*, meaning "divine-work." These were rituals intended to unite the practitioner with the divine.</note> and are explained here—has, for the most part, been misunderstood since its destruction. It has typically been viewed only in its degraded forms among "barbaric" nations, or during the decline and fall of the Roman Empire. As that empire became overwhelmed by corruption, this theology gradually fell with it, until it eventually vanished from what is commonly called the civilized part of the world. This will be clear to the intelligent reader from the following remarks. These points are a summary <note>original: "epitome"</note> of what I have discussed at greater length elsewhere, and they demonstrate that the religions of the **Chaldeans**, **Egyptians**, and **Greeks** were no less scientific than they were spiritually grand.

First, this theology celebrates a vast, singular principle of all things. It views this principle as something even higher than existence itself—something that stands apart from the entire universe, even though it is the source of everything in a way that words cannot describe <note>original: "ineffably"</note>; and

<summary>This page introduces the concept of theurgy as a "scientific" and "sublime" religious practice and begins to describe the Neoplatonic view of a supreme first principle that exists beyond being itself.</summary>

Indeed, it even apologizes for applying the names of our simplest concepts to that which exists beyond all knowledge and all understanding. It names this principle, however, *the one* and *the good*; using the first name to indicate its ultimate simplicity, and the second

* According to this theology, as I have shown elsewhere, in every order of things, a triad is the immediate offspring of a monad <note>A single, indivisible source or "one."</note>. Thus, the "intelligible triad" <note>The highest grouping of three that can be grasped by the mind.</note> emerges immediately from the unspeakable <note>original: "ineffable"</note> principle of all things. Phanes <note>A primary deity in Orphic tradition representing light and creation.</note>, or the "intelligible intellect," who is the final part of this intelligible order, is the monad, the leader, and the producing cause of another triad, which is called <term>intelligible and intellectual</term> <note>original: "νοητὸς καὶ νοερὸς" (noētos kai noeros). This describes a bridge between pure thought and the act of thinking.</note>. In the same way, the very end of this order produces from itself the "intellectual triad": Saturn, Rhea, and Jupiter. Again, Jupiter, who is also the Demiurgus <note>The "Divine Architect" or "Craftsman" of the universe.</note>, is the monad of the "supermundane triad" <note>A group of three that exists above the physical world.</note>. Apollo, who exists at the furthest end of the supermundane order, produces a triad of <term>liberated Gods</term> <note>original: "Θεοὶ ἀπόλυτοι" (Theoi apolytoi). These are deities who are not bound to specific physical locations or celestial bodies.</note>. Finally, the furthest end of this liberated order becomes the monad for a triad of "mundane Gods" <note>Deities who oversee the physical, material world.</note>. This theory, which is the product of the most perfect science, is in complete agreement with the **Chaldean** <note>Referring to the ancient wisdom of the Neo-Babylonian/Persian region.</note> theology. For this reason, it is stated in one of the Chaldean Oracles:
> "In every world a triad shines forth, of which a monad is the ruling principle."

For those readers who wish to be fully convinced of this, I recommend my translation of **Proclus** <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher who systematized these ideas in the 5th century AD.</note> on the *Theology of Plato*.

<meta>This page continues the logical deduction from page x. Having established the "One" as the primary source, it now argues for a "Chain of Being" where existence flows continuously without gaps, governed by the rule that like causes produce like effects.</meta>

<page-num>xi</page-num>

It is necessary that the progression of beings <note>The hierarchical sequence of existence, descending from the divine source to the physical world.</note> should be continued, and that no vacuum <note>A gap or empty space in the continuity of existence.</note> should intervene either in incorporeal <note>Non-physical or spiritual entities, such as the soul or intellect.</note> or corporeal <note>Physical or material bodies.</note> natures. It is also necessary that every thing which has a natural progression should proceed through similitude <note>The principle that an effect must resemble its cause.</note>. In consequence of this, it is likewise necessary that every producing principle <note>A fundamental cause that brings something else into being.</note> should generate a number of the same order with itself: namely, ***nature*** produces a natural number; ***soul*** produces one that is psychical (*i. e.* belonging to the soul); and ***intellect*** produces an intellectual number. 

For if whatever possesses a power of generating produces things that are similar to itself before it produces things that are dissimilar, then every cause must deliver its own form and characteristic peculiarity to its progeny. Before it generates that which gives subsistence <note>The state of having a distinct, independent existence.</note> to progressions that are far distant and separate from its own nature, it must first constitute things that are proximate <note>Closest or most immediate.</note> to itself according to essence <note>The fundamental nature or "what-ness" of a thing.</note>, and conjoined with it through similitude. It is, therefore, necessary from these premises—since there is one unity, the principle of the universe—that this unity should produce from itself, prior to every thing else, a multitude of natures characterized

What is it that distinguishes <term>dæmons<note>In ancient Greek philosophy, a *daemon* was not an evil "demon," but a powerful intermediary spirit that acted as a bridge between the high gods and humanity.</note></term> from the visible and invisible Gods, since the visible are connected with the invisible Gods?

These were rituals and prayers designed to bridge the gap between humans and the divine, often through the use of sacred symbols and names.</note>? And whether the soul does not devise great things from casual circumstances? Moreover, there are certain other methods which are conversant with the prediction of future events. And, perhaps, those who possess divine divination, foresee indeed what will happen, yet are not on this account...

## CHAPTER II.

WE will, therefore, present to you the specific teachings of the Assyrians <note>In this context, "Assyrians" refers to the Chaldeans, ancient sages of Mesopotamia renowned for their astronomical and spiritual wisdom.</note>; and we will also clearly explain our own views to you. We have gathered these insights partly from the vast writings of the ancients, and partly from those specific details which the ancients compiled into a single work regarding the complete knowledge of divine matters. If you propose any philosophical inquiry, we will discuss it for you according to the ancient pillars of Hermes <note>According to Egyptian tradition, the god Hermes Trismegistus—or Thoth—recorded all sacred knowledge on stone pillars to preserve it for eternity.</note>, which Plato and Pythagoras were familiar with before us, and from which they built their own philosophies. 

However, for those questions that involve foreign ideas, or which are contradictory and argumentative, we will address them gently and appropriately, or we will demonstrate their absurdity. Likewise, for those matters that align * with <term>common conceptions</term> <note>Universal ideas or "common sense" principles that are naturally present in the human mind.</note>, we will attempt to discuss them in a way that is perfectly familiar and clear. Finally, for those subjects that require actual experience in <term>divine operations</term> <note>Theurgy, or "divine work," which involves rituals intended to connect the soul with the divine, rather than just intellectual study.</note> to be understood accurately, we will explain them as far as is possible to do so with words alone; but such as are—

In a similar way, we will examine all other topics methodically and as befits their nature.

# CHAPTER III.

In the first place, therefore, you say, "*it must be granted that there are Gods.*" To speak in this way, however, is not correct when discussing this subject. For an innate knowledge of the Gods is co-existent with our very essence; and this knowledge is superior to all judgment and deliberate choice, and exists prior to reason and demonstration. It is also united from the beginning with its own proper cause, and exists alongside the essential tendency of the soul toward *the good*. 

If, indeed, it is necessary to speak the truth, the contact with divinity is not "knowledge" in the traditional sense. For knowledge is, in a certain respect, separated from its object by <term>otherness</term> <note>The concept of "otherness" (*heterotes*) implies a gap or distinction between the person who knows and the thing being known. He also writes "that the contact as of one with one is above knowledge." Elsewhere, he states "the intellectual perception of the first <term>intelligible</term> <note>The "intelligible" refers to the highest realm of reality, which can only be understood by the pure intellect or spirit, rather than the physical senses.</note> is without any difference or distinction." <note>original: "Damascius περι αρχων... ετεροτητος μη ουσης, μηδε γνωσις εσται. Et συναφη ως ενος προς εν, υπερ γνωσιν. Alibi, αδιακριτος η του πρωτου νοητου νοησις."</note></margin> But prior to the knowledge which allows one thing to know another is the uniform connection with divinity—a connection which is suspended from the Gods, and is spontaneous and inseparable from them. Hence, it is not proper to "grant" this as if it were a choice, as

## CHAPTER IV.

WITH respect to your inquiry, “*what the **peculiarities** <note>The specific, distinguishing characteristics or unique traits.</note> are in each of the more excellent **genera** <term>genera: the plural of genus; refers to the different classes or categories of higher beings</term>, by which they are separated from each other?*” if you understand by "peculiarities" the **specific differences** <note>In logic, these are the traits that divide a general category into specific groups, like how "reason" distinguishes humans from other animals.</note> under the same genus, which are distinguished by opposite qualities—such as the "rational" and "irrational" under the category of "animal"—we by no means admit peculiarities of this kind in things which neither have one common **essence** <term>essence: the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing that makes it what it is</term>, nor an equal **contradistinction** <note>A direct, balanced opposition between two things of the same level.</note>, nor receive a composition from something common which is indefinite and then defines the peculiarity. But if you understand the peculiarity to be, as in **prior and secondary natures** <note>Higher-ranking beings (like Gods) versus lower-ranking beings (like daemons or heroes) in the cosmic hierarchy.</note>, differing in their whole essence and whole genus, a certain simple condition of being, definite in itself; in this case,

<meta>This page continues the critique of Porphyry's method for distinguishing between divine beings. It argues that to understand the differences between Gods, daemons, and heroes, one must look at their fundamental nature and power, not just their external actions. It specifically rejects the idea that divine beings experience "passion" or are acted upon by external forces.</meta>

<page-num>->27<-</page-num>

your conception of **peculiarities** <note>The specific, distinguishing characteristics or unique traits that define a particular class of being.</note> will be reasonable. For these peculiarities of things, which have an **eternal subsistence** <term>eternal subsistence: a state of being that exists forever and is not dependent on anything else for its continued existence</term>, are simple, and entirely exempt. The inquiry, however, proceeds imperfectly. For it was necessary, in the first place, to inquire what the peculiarities are of the **more excellent genera** <note>The higher classes of divine beings, such as Gods, angels, daemons, and heroes.</note>, according to **essence** <term>essence: the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing—what it actually is</term>; in the next place, what they are according to **power** <term>power: the internal capacity or potential for action inherent in a nature</term>; and thus afterwards, what they are according to **energy** <term>energy: the active manifestation or outward work of a being’s power</term>. 

But, as your question now stands, with respect to the peculiarities by which these **genera** <term>genera: classes or categories of beings</term> are separated, you alone speak of the peculiarities of energies. Hence you inquire concerning the difference in the last things pertaining to them <note>Meaning, the author believes Porphyry is only looking at the final "symptoms" or results of divine activity rather than their primary causes.</note>; but you leave uninvestigated such things as are first, and most honourable in them, and which are the elements of their difference.

For your question asks, “*How are **essences** <term>essences: the fundamental nature or "what-ness" of a being</term> known by **energies** <term>energies: the active expressions or outward workings of a power</term>, by physical motions, and by **accidents**?*” <term>accidents: properties that a thing may or may not have without losing its core identity (e.g., being tall or sitting down)</term>

The very contrary, however, to all this takes place. For if energies and motions were what defined essences, they would be the masters of the difference which exists between them. But if essences generate energies—the former being separate and existing prior to the latter—then it is the essences that give to motions, energies, and accidents the characteristics by which they differ from each other. This, therefore, works in the opposite way to what you suppose for the purpose of discovering the specific traits you are now investigating.

In short, whether you think that there is one **genus** <term>genus: a broad category or class of beings</term> of the Gods, one of **dæmons** <note>In this context, daemons are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits between gods and humans.</note>, and in a similar manner of **heroes**, and souls that are essentially **incorporeal** <gloss>existing without physical bodies</gloss>; or whether you admit that these are several different groups, you are asking what their difference is based on their unique traits. 

For if you believe that each of these is one and the same category, the whole arrangement of **scientific theology** <note>original: "scientific theology"—this refers to the systematic and rational study of divine hierarchies.</note> is thrown into confusion. But if, as truth requires, you admit that they are distinguished by their categories, and that they do not share one common essential definition—but rather that those which are higher are exempt from those that are inferior—it is not possible to discover common boundaries between them. ## CHAP. VII.

Of these extremes, one is supreme, <term>transcendent</term> <note>transcendent: existing above and independent of the physical universe</note>, and perfect; the other is last in rank, lacking, and more imperfect. The former is capable of accomplishing all things at once, uniformly and in an instant. The latter, however, is not able to do all things, nor can it act all at once, nor suddenly, nor as a single, undivided whole. 

The former also generates and governs all things without being pulled down toward them or affected by them; but the latter is naturally inclined to lean toward and be focused on the things that it generates and governs. Furthermore, the former—as the <term>primordial</term> <note>primordial: existing at the very beginning; the original source of everything else</note> cause—precedes all things in power. The latter, being dependent on the will of the <term>Gods</term> <note>Gods: in this philosophical tradition, these are the highest, most unified divine principles</note> as its cause, has existed from eternity <term>consubsistent</term> <note>consubsistent: existing together with or dependent upon the same substance; here, it means the lower being’s existence is tied directly to the divine will</note> with that will. 

Likewise, the former, through a single and vigorous <term>acme</term> <note>acme: the highest point or peak of power and vitality</note>, contains within itself the goals of all <term>energies</term> <note>energies: the active powers or outward operations of a being</note> and <term>essences</term> <note>essences: the fundamental nature or core reality of a thing</note>; but the latter passes from one state to another, moving from some things toward others.

But the **soul** has certain distinct boundaries, which mark the limits of its dominion. 

Since these are the different characteristics of the two extremes <note>the Gods at the top and the Soul at the bottom</note>, it will not be difficult to understand what we have said, and to perceive the middle characteristics of <term>dæmons</term> <note>dæmons: from the Greek *daimones*, these are intermediary spirits or guiding entities, not to be confused with modern "demons"</note> and <term>heroes</term> <note>heroes: in this context, souls of great power that act as intermediaries between dæmons and humans</note>. These middle beings are allied to each of the extremes; they possess a likeness to each, yet they move away from both toward the middle. They embrace a harmonious connection that blends qualities from both extremes and links them together in balanced proportions. Such, therefore, must be the way we understand the unique characteristics of the first <term>divine genera</term> <note>divine genera: the different classes or categories of divine beings</note>.

### CHAP. XIV.

**FARTHER** still, with respect to “*what are called the necessities of the Gods,*” <note>Critics of religion often argued that if Gods are bound by "necessity" (rules or fate), they are not truly all-powerful. But from supplication, we are in a short time led to the object of supplication, acquire its similitude <note>The state of becoming similar to or reflecting the qualities of the divine.</note> from intimate converse, and gradually obtain divine perfection, instead of our own imbecility <note>In this historical context, this refers to a state of human weakness or lack of spiritual strength, rather than a lack of intelligence.</note> and imperfection.

## CHAPTER XVIII.

Your next inquiry doubts, “*how some of the Gods are beneficent, but others malefic.*” <note>original: "benefici... malefici"</note> This opinion, therefore, is assumed from the <term>predictors of nativities<gloss>ancient astrologers who cast birth charts to predict a person's destiny</gloss></term>. It is, however, entirely remote from the truth. For all the Gods are good, and invariably the causes of good; and all of them are uniformly <term>convolved<gloss>literally "rolled together"; united in a single movement or purpose</gloss></term> toward the one good, according to the "beautiful and good" alone. 

The bodies, likewise, which are subject to them <note>The author refers to the physical planets and stars which are moved by the Gods.</note> possess immense powers; some of which are firmly established in the divine bodies themselves, but others proceed from them into the nature of the world, and into the world itself, descending in an orderly manner through the whole of <term>generation<gloss>the physical realm of birth, change, and decay</gloss></term>, and extending without impediment as far as to things which have a <term>partial subsistence<gloss>existence as individual, fragmented parts of the whole, such as humans, animals, or plants</gloss></term>.

With respect to the powers, therefore, which remain in the heavens in the divine bodies themselves, there can be no doubt that all of them are similar. Hence, it remains that we should discuss those powers which are transmitted from the heavens to us, and are mingled with the realm of generation. These, therefore, descend with invariable sameness for the salvation of the universe, and one order. It also imitates a divine life, by the life which is <term>connascent<gloss>naturally born with or inseparable from</gloss></term> with <term>ethereal<gloss>composed of "aether," the pure, fifth element believed to make up the heavens</gloss></term> bodies.

...and they contain the entire process of <term>generation<gloss>the cycle of birth, change, and decay in the physical world</gloss></term> in a unified and connected way. These divine forces are also <term>impassive<gloss>incapable of being harmed, changed, or moved by outside influences</gloss></term> and unchanging, even though they extend their influence into our world, which is constantly changing and being affected by others.

Since the realm of generation is diverse and made of many different parts, it receives *the one* <note>original: "to hen"; a reference to the Neoplatonic concept of the ultimate, unified source of all existence</note> of the Gods—and that part of them which is without any internal difference—through a lens of conflict and division. This happens because the material world follows its own nature of opposition and fragmentation.

It also receives that which is "impassive" in a "passive" or suffering way; in short, the material world shares in the divine according to its own limited nature, and not according to the true, unlimited power of the Gods.

Therefore, just as something that is "generated" (or exists within the state of "becoming") shares in pure "Being" only through the act of being born, and just as a physical body experiences the "incorporeal" (non-physical) only in a physical way, so too do the physical and material substances of our world share in the immaterial and <term>etherial<gloss>referring to the "aether," the pure, celestial substance that makes up the heavens</gloss></term> bodies—which exist far above nature and the cycle of change—in a confused and disorganized manner.

Because of this, it is absurd for people to think that <term>intelligible forms<gloss>the perfect, abstract "blueprints" of things existing in the divine mind</gloss></term> have color, shape, or physical touch just because the objects on earth that reflect them have those qualities. Likewise, it is wrong for people to blame the <term>celestial bodies<gloss>the stars and planets, which were viewed as the physical vehicles of divine beings</gloss></term> for being "wicked" or "evil," simply because the people or things on Earth that receive their influence sometimes produce bad results.

For the divine influence coming from the source could not be an evil thing, unless the recipient had some <term>mutation<gloss>a change, corruption, or defect in the receiver's nature</gloss></term>.

## CHAPTER IV.

Moving, therefore, to other unique characteristics of these beings, we say that among the **Gods**, there is a sharpness and speed in their <term>energies<gloss>In this context, "energies" refers to the active power or outward operation of a divine being.</gloss></term> which shine forth even faster than <term>intellect<gloss>original: nous; the divine Mind or the highest level of rational thought.</gloss></term> itself, even though the Gods themselves remain unchanging and stable. With **archangels**, this speed is, in a certain way, blended with their powerful activities. The actions of **angels** involve a certain degree of motion, and they do not possess a power that works simply through speech in the same way archangels do. The activities of <term>dæmons<gloss>Intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between the divine and the earthly; not to be confused with the modern concept of "demons."</gloss></term> appear to be faster than they actually are. In the movements of the <term>phasmata<gloss>Manifestations or apparitions that appear to the practitioner during a ritual.</gloss></term> of **heroes**, a certain sense of grandeur is visible; however, in carrying out their desires, their actions are not as swift as those of <term>dæmons</term>. In the <term>phasmata</term> of <term>archons<gloss>Rulers or governors of the lower material realms and planetary spheres.</gloss></term>, the primary activities appear to be most excellent and commanding; but their secondary actions have a more visible presence, yet they fail to achieve their intended goal. Finally, the <term>phasmata</term> of **souls** are seen to be more restless and changeable, yet they are more <term>imbecile<gloss>In the archaic sense: weak, powerless, or lacking in spiritual strength.</gloss></term> than those of the heroes.

Gods reveal true images of themselves, but they by no means project <term>phantasms</term> <note>original: phantasmata; deceptive or illusory appearances that lack true reality, much like reflections in water or mirrors.</note> of themselves, such as those that exist in water or in mirrors. It does not, however, recognize them because it is prompted by our human intelligence; for it is not natural that things which encompass everything should be prompted by those that are encompassed, nor that perfect natures be moved by imperfect ones, nor wholes by their parts.

Hence, divine causes are not previously called into action by our <term>acts of thought</term> <note>original: *intellections*.</note>; rather, it is necessary to consider these thoughts, along with the best dispositions of our soul and our own purity, as certain <term>auxiliary causes</term> <note>original: *concauses*; secondary factors that assist but do not direct the primary power.</note>. The things that properly awaken the divine will are the divine symbols themselves. And thus, things pertaining to the Gods are moved by the Gods themselves, and they do not receive the starting principle of their own activity from any inferior nature.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I have, however, been thus **detailed** <note>original: *prolix*.</note> in order that you may not think all the authority of the power in <term>theurgic rituals</term> <note>original: *theurgic operations*; the practice of sacred rites to connect with the divine.</note> is in our power, and that you may not suppose the true work of them consists in our mental concepts, or that their failure results from our own deception. For though we may know the specific traits which belong to each <term>class of being</term> <note>original: *genus*; referring to the different categories of spirits, dæmons, or gods.</note>, we still may not obtain...

### CHAP. I.

In the first place, therefore, you ask me to explain to you clearly, “***what is it that occurs during the foreknowledge of future events?***” Right away, however, what you are trying to learn is impossible. For, based on the way you phrased your question, you seem to think that <term>foreknowledge</term> <note>original: praenotio; the ability to perceive future events through divine connection.</note> is something produced by a cause, or something that exists as a process of "becoming," and belongs to things that have a natural existence. 

It is not, however, one of those things which exist by coming into being, nor does it happen through <term>physical mutation</term> <note>A natural change or biological process in the material world.</note>. It was not invented and devised as something merely useful for the purposes of life; in short, it is not a human work. Instead, it is divine and supernatural, sent down to us from the heavens above. It is also <term>unbegotten</term> <note>Existing eternally without being created or born.</note> and eternal, and spontaneously possesses a <term>precedaneous subsistence</term> <note>An existence that is primary and exists before all other dependent things.</note>.

The greatest remedy, therefore, for all such doubts is this: to know the fundamental principle of <term>divination</term> <note>The practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown through divine or supernatural means.</note>—

### CHAPTER V.

**THERE** are many types of <term>divine possession</term> <note>Also known as 'theolepsy,' this is the state of being inhabited or controlled by a deity.</note>, and divine inspiration is sparked in many different ways; because of this, the signs of it are many and varied. This is either because the Gods who inspire us are different—thus producing different types of inspiration—or because the various methods of triggering these <term>enthusiasms</term> <note>From the Greek 'enthousiasmos,' meaning 'having a god within.'</note> produce a different <term>afflatus</term> <note>A Latin term meaning 'breath' or 'blast,' used here to describe a sudden burst of divine influence or 'divine breath.'</note>.

In some cases, the deity possesses us entirely; in others, we surrender ourselves completely to the deity; and sometimes, we share a unified activity with them. Sometimes we participate in the lowest level of divine power, sometimes in the middle level, and sometimes in the highest. At certain times, there is a simple participation in the divine; at other times, a shared communion; and sometimes, a complete union of these divine inspirations. Furthermore, the inspiration might be experienced by the soul alone, or the soul may receive it in conjunction with the body, or it may be experienced by the <term>common animal</term> <note>A philosophical term referring to the unified entity of the soul and the physical body acting as a single biological unit.</note> as a whole.

Because of these variations, the signs shown by those who are inspired take many forms. The presence of inspiration is revealed through the movements of the entire body or specific parts of it, or conversely, by the body being in a state of perfect rest. Accordingly, because of these ways that melodies are matched to the Gods, the Gods themselves become present. There is nothing that stands in the way; *so that whatever bears even a chance resemblance to the Gods directly shares in their nature.* A state of perfect possession immediately occurs, along with a fullness of a more excellent essence and power. 

This does not happen because the body and soul are "in sync" or reacting to the music through simple sympathy; rather, it is because the inspiration of the Gods is never truly separated from divine harmony. Because this inspiration is naturally suited and allied to that harmony, it is shared through the music in the proper proportions. For this reason, the inspiration is either stirred up or calmed according to the different ranks <note>The "orders" or hierarchy of the Gods in Neoplatonic philosophy.</note> of the Gods. However, we must never call this inspiration a removal, a cleansing <note>original: "purgation," likely referring to the Aristotelian concept of *catharsis*.</note>, or a medicine. It does not originate in us as a way to treat a disease, an excess, or a surplus; instead, its entire principle and the way we participate in it are derived supernally <note>Derived from above; from the heavens or the divine realm.</note> from the Gods.

It is also incorrect to say that the soul is fundamentally made of harmony and rhythm. If that were true, <term>enthusiasm</term> <note>In this context, the state of being filled with a divine spirit or "divine possession."</note> would belong only to the soul's own nature. It is better to deny this and instead claim that before the soul gave herself over to a body, she was a listener of divine harmony. Thus, when she entered into a body, and heard such melodies as these, she recognized them...

## CHAPTER 10

**LET** us now discuss the specifics of prophecy in more detail. We should not claim that nature simply leads each thing toward its like, for the power of <term>divine inspiration</term> <note>original: "enthusiastic energy," from the Greek *enthousiasmos*, meaning to be filled with a god.</note> is not a work of nature. Nor should we claim that the temperature of the air, or of the environment around us, produces a change in the physical temperature of those experiencing this divine state. Since inspiration is the work of the Gods, it is not altered by physical forces or the body’s temperament. 

Furthermore, we must not say that this famous divine inspiration is subject to human emotions or the laws of the physical world. The gift of the Gods’ own power to humanity is <term>impassive</term> <note>Unaffected by external influence, suffering, or human emotion.</note> and superior to the entire realm of birth and decay. ### CHAPTER XII.

IT appears, therefore, that the divination of oracles accords with all the hypotheses which we have before adduced concerning prediction. For if a power of this kind was inseparable from the nature of places, and of the bodies which are the subjects of it, or proceeded * according to a motion defined by number <note>This refers to the Platonic and Pythagorean idea that physical time and celestial movements are governed by mathematical ratios (number), whereas the divine realm exists outside these constraints.</note>, it would not be able to foreknow, with invariable sameness, things which exist every where and always. But being separate and liberated from places and things which are measured by the numbers of time, and also from those which are detained in place, it is equally present with all things wherever they may be, and subsists simultaneously with all the natures that are produced.

produced according to time. It likewise encompasses the truth of all things within itself, through its separate and transcendent essence <term>transcendent essence: a nature that exists above and beyond the limitations of the physical world</term>.

Hence, if this is rightly asserted by us, the prophetic power of the Gods is not limited by any specific place, nor by a specific human body, nor by the soul (which is confined to one certain type of divisible nature <note>In Platonic philosophy, "divisible natures" refers to physical things that can be broken apart or changed, as opposed to the "indivisible" and eternal divine</note>); but being separate and whole, it is present everywhere with all natures that are capable of receiving it. It likewise illuminates from the outside and fills all things, pervades through all the elements—earth and air, fire and water—and leaves nothing without its presence, neither animals nor any of the productions of nature. Instead, it grants from itself a certain portion of foreknowledge to some things in a greater degree, and to others in a less. Moreover, existing before all things by its own independent nature, it is sufficient to fill all things as much as each is able to participate in it.

* <margin>This assertion, that the nature which is perfectly <term>exempt</term> <note>Exempt: In this philosophy, "exempt" means a higher reality is entirely set apart from and untainted by the lower things it influences.</note> can never become one with that which departs from itself, is opposed by Thomas Gale. He claims that man is composed of soul and body, even though the body is far inferior to the soul. But in using this example, Gale clearly shows he does not understand Iamblichus. The human soul is a "middle ground" between an indivisible and a divisible essence; because it shares in that divisible essence, it has a natural alliance with the body and is not perfectly exempt from it. However, this is not the case for divine inspiration and our soul, for the divine transcends the soul in a perfectly exempt manner. Let it be granted, as Michael Psellus says, that a "<term>hypostatic union</term>" <note>Hypostatic union: A term often used in theology to describe how two different natures (like the divine and the human) might be joined into one single existence.</note> brings different natures into one <term>hypostasis</term>. Yet such a union can never happen between two things where one has no natural connection, proximity, or alliance to the other. Gale was led into this mistake by not paying attention to the words "perfectly exempt" <note>original Greek: "το παντελῶς ἐξῃρημένον"</note> which Iamblichus uses here. Such mistakes are common for Gale, due to his messy and unfocused way of thinking. He also forgot, while writing these notes, that he was merely a headmaster of a grammar school and not a philosopher.</margin>

From what has been said, the absurdity of the opinion held by those who imagine the divine essence can be mingled and united with mortal nature is immediately obvious. For if such a union were possible, it would benefit and lift up the mortal nature, but it would harm and degrade the divine essence. 

Just as in the union of the rational soul with the body (as Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was one of the last major Greek philosophers and a head of the Platonic Academy in Athens.</note> beautifully observes in his commentary on the *Timaeus* <note>The Timaeus is one of Plato’s most famous dialogues, focusing on the creation of the universe and the nature of the soul.</note>, page 339), "the soul, by turning toward a material life, certainly lights a flame in the body, but she herself becomes situated in darkness; and by giving life to the body, she destroys both herself and her own intellect" [at least as much as such eternal things are capable of receiving destruction].

### CHAP. XXII.

You say, therefore, “*that the soul generates the power which has an imaginative perception of futurity, through motions of this kind,* <note>The author is quoting his opponent, Porphyry, who suggested that the soul might create its own ability to see the future through its own internal movements or psychological states.</note>

<note>
The scholar Thomas Gale <note>Thomas Gale (1635–1702) was an English classicist who edited the Latin edition of this text.</note> correctly guesses that when Iamblichus uses the word *both* here, he is referring to the combination of the soul and divine inspiration coming from the outside. However, Gale is mistaken when he argues that inspiration cannot be eternal because it is a "transient energy of God." Gale shows himself to be a poor theologian and philosopher here. Because God is an eternal—or rather, a <term>supereternal</term> <note>Existing beyond or above the very concept of time and eternity.</note>—nature, His actions (energies) are not bound by time or gradual progress. Instead, they are "stably simultaneous" (existing all at once). The "transition" or change does not happen within the divine influence itself, but within the human beings who receive it, because we are temporary and subject to change. It is as illogical to call God’s energy "transient" as it would be to say the sun’s light is "transient" simply because it shines through <term>diaphanous</term> <note>Transparent or clear; allowing light to pass through.</note> materials but is blocked by solid ones. The change is in the objects, not the light.

Just as those who commit sacrilege are the greatest enemies to the religious worship of the Gods, so too are those who deal with deceptive **spirits** <note>original: "dæmons"; in this context, referring to lower, often meddlesome spiritual entities rather than "demons" in the modern sense.</note> and the causes of lack of self-control—they are undoubtedly enemies to **theurgists** <note>original: "theurgists"; practitioners of "god-working," or rituals intended to unite the soul with the divine.</note>. 

For every corrupt spirit flees from these practitioners, and when they are present, such spirits are completely defeated. Every vice and every passion is totally cut away by these rituals; for a pure participation in the "Good" is available to those who are pure, and they are filled from above with truth from a **divine fire**. These practitioners, therefore, suffer no hindrance from evil spirits, nor are these spirits any obstacle to the well-being of their souls. 

Nor are theurgists disturbed by pride, or flattery, or the enjoyment of **sacrificial vapors** <note>original: "exhalations"; likely referring to the material smoke or steam from offerings which lower, "material" spirits were thought to feed upon.</note>, or any violence; instead, all these things, as if struck by lightning, pull back and retreat without touching the theurgist or even being able to approach them. 

Hence, this kind of divination is unpolluted and **priestly** <note>original: "sacerdotal"</note>; it is truly divine. This also does not, as you suggest, require me or anyone else to act as a **judge** <note>original: "arbiter"</note> in order for me to rank it above a multitude of other things. Instead, it is itself set apart from all things; it is supernatural and has existed eternally, neither...

## CHAPTER II.

<margin>These spirits without reason are more excellent than we are because they serve the needs of the whole universe; however, because they lack reason, they are also inferior to us.</margin>

BUT we sometimes see that take place which is now proposed to be considered. For it happens that spirits are commanded to perform tasks even though they do not use a reason of their own and lack the principle of judgment. Nor does this happen without a logical cause. For our <term>dianoia</term> <note>original: "dianoia"; refers to the discursive or reasoning part of the human mind which processes information step-by-step.</note> naturally possesses the power of reasoning about and judging things as they truly are. Because it contains many different vital powers within itself, it is accustomed to commanding these most irrational spirits—those which derive their perfection from a single type of activity alone. 

Hence, the human mind invokes these spirits as more excellent beings because it seeks to draw down certain things from the whole world <note>The "Whole" or the "Universal" refers to the entire cosmos as a single living organism.</note> into specific, individual circumstances. These spirits are vital because they contribute to the functioning of the "wholes" in which we are contained. Yet, the mind also commands them as inferior beings because certain parts of the world—such as our own <term>reasoning power</term>—are often more pure and perfect than the entities that merely extend themselves across the physical world. 

Thus, for instance, if one thing is intellectual <note>In this context, "intellectual" means related to the higher mind or divine intellect, rather than just "smart."</note> (as is the case with our <term>dianoia</term>), but another is entirely without a soul or purely physical, then

## CHAPTER IV.

I am of the opinion that what appears to us to be an accurate definition of **justice** does not appear the same way to the Gods. (videlicet)</note>, that of spirits—so it is with matters of justice and injustice. Beauty and justice are to be attributed only to the Gods and good spirits; however, those spirits that are naturally depraved commit what is unjust and shameful. 

Indeed, that which is consistent, in harmony with itself, and remains eternally the same belongs to the higher, more excellent natures. Conversely, that which is self-conflicting, discordant, and never the same is the defining characteristic of spirit-driven <note>original: "dæmoniacal"</note> conflict. It is not at all surprising that opposing forces exist within such natures; in fact, it would be far more surprising if they did not.

## CHAP. VIII.

WE may, however, beginning from another <term>hypothesis</term> <note>A starting assumption or premise for a logical argument.</note>, demonstrate the same thing. We must admit that the <term>corporeal parts</term> <note>The material or physical elements of the cosmos, such as the planets and the natural elements.</note> of the universe are neither sluggish nor destitute of power, but as much as they excel our concerns in perfection, beauty, and magnitude, by so much also is the power which is present with them greater. Each, likewise, by itself is capable of effecting different things, and produces certain different energies. They are also capable of effecting things much more numerous on each other. And besides this, a certain multiform production extends to parts from <term>wholes</term> <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, "wholes" are the complete, universal systems (like the entire Sky or the Earth) that govern individual "parts" (like a single person or a rock).</note>; partly from <term>sympathy</term> <note>original: "sympathia". This refers to a "cosmic resonance" where things are naturally connected and affected by one another due to their shared properties.</note>, through <term>similitude of powers</term> <note>The principle that things with similar qualities naturally influence or attract one another.</note>, and partly from the aptitude of the <term>agent</term> <note>The entity performing an action or exertng influence.</note> to the <term>patient</term> <note>The entity receiving the action or being influenced.</note>. 

If, therefore, certain evils and destructions happen to parts, they are salutary and good as with reference to wholes and the <term>harmony of the universe</term>, but to parts they introduce a necessary <term>corruption</term> <note>In this context, the breaking down or changing of a physical form; decay.</note>, either from not being able to bear the energies of wholes, or from a certain other commixture and temperament of their own <term>imbecility</term> <note>The inherent frailty, weakness, or limited capacity of material objects compared to divine ones.</note>, or, in the third place, from the privation of <term>symmetry</term> <note>A lack of balance or proportion.</note> in the parts to each other.

<summary>This chapter argues that the physical universe is a powerful, interconnected system where what appears "evil" or destructive to an individual part is actually necessary for the greater good and harmony of the whole.</summary>

## CHAP. IX.

AFTER the body of the universe, also, many things are generated by its very nature. ### CHAP. I.

The doubt mentioned by you in the next place is, as I might say, an inquiry made in common by both the learned and the unlearned; I am referring to the matter of **sacrifices**. You ask, “*what utility or power they possess in the universe, and with the Gods, and for what reason they are performed—appropriate, indeed, to the powers who are honored by them, but useful to those by whom the gifts are offered.*” In the same passage, another objection is raised: “*that the interpreters of prophecies and oracles ought to abstain from animals, lest the Gods should be polluted by the vapours arising from them. For this is contrary to the assertion that the Gods are especially allured by the vapours of animals.*” <note>The author is addressing a classic paradox: if gods are pure, why would they want the smoky, meaty "vapours" of a burnt offering? And if they do like those vapours, why must priests stay "pure" by not eating meat?</note>

---

### CHAP. II.

The hostile opposition, therefore, found in these proposals may be easily dissolved by demonstrating the dignity of <term>wholes</term> <note>In this philosophical context, "wholes" refers to the universal, complete systems of the cosmos, which operate differently than individual "parts" like humans.</note> with respect to their power in <term>generation</term> <note>The process of coming-into-being, or the physical world of change and decay.</note>, in human affairs, and in those things that exist around the earth. Therefore, why is it surprising that a class of this kind should produce such effects? For not every man is able to distinguish a good from an evil <term>daemon</term> <note>original: "dæmon". An intermediate spirit; not necessarily "demon" in the modern evil sense, but a guiding or mediating power.</note>, or to tell by what specific traits one is separated from the other. Consequently, those who are not able to perceive the difference between the two reason absurdly regarding their cause; they attribute this cause to <term>genera</term> <note>Classes or categories of being.</note> superior to nature and the <term>demoniacal order</term> <note>The hierarchy of spirits that exist between the earthly realm and the highest divine realm.</note>.

### CHAPTER IV.

Nor is there any real difficulty in the matter that disturbs you so much and which you argue for so vigorously—I mean <term>abstinence from animals</term> <note>Refers to the practice of vegetarianism, which was a major point of spiritual and ethical debate in the ancient world.</note>—provided it is understood correctly. ### CHAPTER V.

Your next inquiry is of greater consequence, and concerns matters of a more sublime nature. How, then, shall I be able to give you a brief and sufficient answer to a question that is extremely difficult and requires a long explanation? Nevertheless, I will answer it, and I will do so with great readiness. I will also endeavor to follow the points you have briefly indicated and quietly suggested. 

I will now unfold to you my <term>dogma</term> <note>original: "dogma." In this philosophical context, it refers to a formal system of principles or a settled way of thinking about the divine.</note> concerning <term>sacrifices</term> <note>Ritual offerings made to spiritual beings as part of ancient religious practice.</note> [which is as follows]: 

It is by no means necessary that sacrifices should be offered for the sake of honor alone, in the same way that we honor human benefactors. Nor should they be offered simply to return thanks for the goods granted to us by the <term>Gods</term>; nor even as an offering of "first fruits," or as a way of paying back the Gods for the more sacred blessings they bestow on us. Such motives are common to human relationships and are borrowed from the standard <term>polity</term> <note>original: "polity." This refers to the organizational structure or social rules of a human community.</note> of mankind. These human-centered reasons fail to preserve the <term>transcendency</term> <note>The quality of being completely above and independent of the material world.</note> of the Gods or their order as <term>exempt causes</term> <note>An "exempt cause" is a creative force that remains separate from its effects; it acts upon the world without being affected by it or tied to it.</note>.

## CHAPTER VI.

**BUT** the most important aspect of <term>sacrifices</term>—namely, their **efficacious power** <note>The actual ability of a ritual to produce a physical or spiritual result.</note>—is something your current view fails to capture. This power is the reason sacrifices are so incredibly beneficial. Without them, we would not be freed from plagues, famines, or the failure of crops, nor would we receive the rain we need in its proper season. Even more importantly, sacrifices provide benefits much greater than these: they contribute to the **purification of the soul** and its **emancipation from generation** <note>original: "emancipation from generation." This refers to the soul being set free from the cycle of physical birth and death, allowing it to return to a higher, divine state.</note>.

The types of sacrifices you have mentioned do not indicate these powers at all. Therefore, no one can rightly approve of such views, because they assign reasons for the rituals that are beneath the dignity of the work being performed. Even if someone were to accept those common explanations, they would only be secondary; they depend entirely on more ancient, primary, and venerable causes.

<margin>\* The number sixty is no less obvious in the crocodile than in the sun. For according to Aristotle (in *History of Animals*, book 5) the crocodile produces sixty white eggs and sits on them for sixty days.</margin>

<margin>† “Isis,” says Gale <note>Likely referring to Thomas Gale (1635–1702), an English classical scholar.</note>, “is the moon. And a dog accompanied Isis when she was diligently searching for her husband Osiris. But the moon constantly seeks the sun, and therefore that clever animal, the dog, corresponds with Isis. In the ceremonies of Isis, dogs also led the procession.” In this way, others besides Gale—who have not reached the deeper levels of the philosophy and theology of Plato—would certainly explain the myths told about Isis. In reality, however, Isis is not the moon, but one of the divine beings that move within the lunar sphere as a companion to the moon; in modern terms, she is one of the satellites of that planet. For, as I have shown from Proclus <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (412–485 AD) who headed the Academy in Athens.</note>, in the introduction to my translation of Plato's *Timaeus*, every planetary sphere is a <term>wholeness</term> <note>original: "ολοτης" (holotēs). Among these satellites, led by the planets, the first in rank are Gods; following them, spirits <note>original: "dæmons" (daimones). In this context, these are not evil beings, but intermediary spirits between gods and humans.</note> move in bright, circular bodies; and these are followed by individual souls, such as ours. See Proclus in his commentary on the *Timaeus*, pages 275 and 279. This theory, as I have noted elsewhere, is the essential key to the theology and mythology of the ancient world, as it shows at a single glance why the same God is so often celebrated with the names of other Gods. This led Macrobius <note>A Latin writer from the 5th century AD who argued that all pagan gods were ultimately representations of the Sun.</note> to believe that all the Gods were merely different powers of the sun. The English reader will find plenty of support for what is said here in the fourth book of my translation of the previously mentioned wonderful work by Proclus.</margin>

being the number 36, was, as is reported, their greatest oath, and was denominated the world. For this number is formed from the composition of the four first even and the four first odd numbers, collected into one sum.* If, therefore, the most approved of the philosophers did not think it proper to neglect or despise any <term>occult</term> <note>hidden or secret</note> signification of a divine nature when they perceived it even in things which are inanimate and incorporeal, it appears to me that they, in a still greater degree, venerated those peculiarities depending on manners which they saw in such natures as had sense, and were endued with soul, with passion, and ethical habits. We must embrace, therefore, not those who honour these things, but those who reverence divinity through these, as through most clear mirrors, and which are produced by nature, in a becoming manner, conceiving them to be the instruments or the art of the God by whom all things are perpetually adorned. But we ought to think that no inanimate being can be more excellent than one that is animated, nor an insensible than a sensitive being, not even though some one should collect together all the gold and emeralds in the universe. For the divinity is not <term>ingenerated</term> <note>innate or born within</note> either in colours, or figures, or smoothness; but such things as neither ever did, nor are naturally adapted to participate of life, have an allotment more ignoble than that of dead bodies. But the nature which lives and sees, and has the principle of motion from itself, and a knowledge of things appropriate and foreign to its being, has certainly derived an <term>efflux</term> <note>an emanation or flowing out</note> and portion of that wisdom which, as Heraclitus <note>A Greek philosopher (c. 535 – 475 BCE) famous for his doctrines of universal change and the "Logos" or cosmic reason.</note> says, considers how both itself and the universe is governed. Hence the divinity is not worse represented in these animals than in the workmanships of copper and stone, which in a similar manner suffer corruption and decay, but are naturally deprived of all sense and consciousness. This then I consider as the best defence that can be given of the adoration of animals by the Egyptians.”

## CHAP. XI.

It appears to me, also, that the present question errs in another respect. For it is ignorant <note>original typo: "ignornant"</note> that the offering of sacrifices through fire has the power of consuming and destroying the matter of them in a greater degree; that it assimilates <note>transforms into a similar nature</note> this matter to itself, but is not itself assimilated to the matter; and that it elevates to divine, celestial, and immaterial fire, but does not tend downwards to matter and <term>generation</term> <note>the cycle of physical birth and decay</note>. For if the enjoyment of the vapors from matter allured <term>dæmons</term> <note>intermediary spirits between the divine and the human</note>, it would be requisite that the matter should be pure and entire; since thus there would be a more abundant <term>efflux</term> <note>a flowing out of particles or energy</note> from it to its participants. 

But now all the matter is enkindled and consumed, and is changed into the purity and <term>tenuity</term> <note>thinness or subtleness of substance</note> of fire; which is itself a clear indication of the contrary to what you assert. For superior beings [i. e. dæmons] are <term>impassive</term> <note>unaffected by external physical sensations or suffering</note>, and they are delighted to amputate <note>to cut away or remove</note> matter through fire, and render us impassive. They likewise assimilate whatever is in us to the Gods, in the same manner as fire * assimilates all solid and resisting sub-

### CHAP. XIII.

**SUBVERTING**, therefore, in this manner the common absurd opinions concerning sacrifices, we shall introduce in their place true conceptions about them. ## CHAP. XIV.

We shall begin the explanation of this subject in the best possible way if we demonstrate how the sacred law of sacrifices is connected to the hierarchy of the Gods. 

In the first place, we say that among the Gods, some are **material** and others are **immaterial**. The material Gods are those who encompass matter within themselves and give it order; the immaterial Gods are those who are perfectly exempt from and transcend matter altogether. 

According to the <term>sacrificial art</term> <note>the traditional system of rituals and offerings used to approach the divine</note>, it is necessary to begin sacred operations with the material Gods; for the ascent to the immaterial Gods cannot be achieved in any other way. The material Gods have a certain communion with matter insofar as they preside over it. Consequently, they have dominion over the things that happen within the realm of matter—such as the division, <term>percussion</term> <note>the physical striking or impact of objects</note>, repercussion, <term>mutation</term> <note>change or transformation</note>, <term>generation, and corruption</term> <note>the philosophical terms for birth/creation and death/decay</note> of all material bodies. 

Therefore, anyone who wishes to worship these beings <term>theurgically</term> <note>from 'theurgy,' meaning 'divine work'; rituals designed to align the human soul with divine powers</note>, in a manner suited to them and to the authority they have been granted, should employ a material mode of worship. For it is only through this approach that we shall be fully led into a familiarity with them, worshipping them in a way that is allied and...

### CHAP. XXI.

## CHAPTER XXIV.

The same principles may also be learned from the way the Gods are distributed according to specific places. From this, and from the **partible dominion** <term>partible dominion</term> <note>The concept that divine authority is divided and assigned to different spheres, such as specific regions of the earth or different parts of the natural world.</note> over each particular thing, we can see how many **allotments** <note>In this context, "allotments" are the specific realms or portions of the universe assigned to various spiritual beings, from high gods to lesser spirits.</note>—some greater and some less—are assigned to superior beings according to their different orders.

For it is evident that to the Gods who preside over certain places, the things produced in those places are the most appropriate offerings in sacrifice. It is naturally fitting that what belongs to the "governed" should be sacrificed to the "governors." To creators, their own works are always particularly pleasing; and to those who are the primary cause of certain things, those specific things are the most acceptable.

Whether we are talking about certain animals, plants, or any other fruits of the earth, if they are governed by superior beings, they simultaneously participate in the **inspective care** <term>inspective care</term> <note>A technical term in Neoplatonism referring to the watchful, protective oversight that a deity provides to the physical world.</note> of those beings and provide us with an **indivisible communion** <note>The idea that ritual acts can bridge the gap between the fragmented material world and the unified, eternal world of the gods.</note> with the Gods. Therefore, if certain things of this kind are carefully preserved, they increase the familiarity of those who keep them with the Gods. These are the things which, by remaining whole and pure, maintain the connection between Gods and men. Of this kind are some of the animals in Egypt, and man himself. <note>The author, Iamblichus, frequently points to the Egyptian tradition as the most ancient and correct form of worship, where specific animals were treated as living links to divine power.</note>

## CHAP. XXV.

**If**, therefore, these things were human customs alone, and derived their authority through our legal institutions, it might be said that the worship of the Gods was the invention of our own conceptions. Now, however, divinity is the leader of it—the one who is thus invoked by sacrifices, and who is surrounded by a numerous multitude of Gods and angels. Under this supreme leader, a certain common presiding power is allotted dominion according to each nation of the earth. And a peculiar presiding power <note>This refers to a localized deity or spirit that "belongs" specifically to one particular temple or holy site.</note> is allotted to each temple. 

Of the sacrifices, also, which are performed to the Gods, the <term>inspective guardian</term> <note>A technical term for a divine being who supervises a ritual to ensure it is performed correctly and reaches its spiritual destination.</note> is a God; but an angel is the guardian of those sacrifices performed to angels; and a <term>dæmon</term> <note>From the Greek "daimon." These are not evil spirits, but intermediary beings who rank between humans and the higher Gods, often managing the affairs of the material world.</note> is the guardian of such as are performed to dæmons. ### CHAP. III.

In the next place, we shall explain how **divination** <term>divination [manteia]</term> <note>The process of obtaining knowledge from a divine source.</note> is accomplished through **sacred animals**, such as, for instance, hawks. We must never say, therefore, that the Gods approach through bodies that are thus procured and employed. For they do not preside over animals either **partibly** <note>In a divided or fragmented way.</note>, or **proximately** <note>Directly and without intermediaries.</note>, or materially, or with a certain **habitude** <term>habitude [schesis]</term> <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, "habitude" refers to a relationship of inclination or disposition toward something, like the soul’s relationship to the body.</note> towards them. 

Instead, this contact with the organs of divination must be attributed to **dæmons** <term>dæmons</term> <note>Benevolent intermediary spirits that rank between gods and humans.</note>—specifically those who are very much "divided" <note>Meaning spirits that are more closely tied to the diversity of the material world.</note>. Different orders of these spirits are allotted to different animals; they exercise a government of this kind directly, and they do not possess their proper **dominion** in a way that is perfectly independent and **immaterial**. Or, if one is willing to admit it, a "seat" must be attributed to them, through which we may be able to associate with and employ them. It is necessary, therefore, to think that this seat should be pure from bodies. For there can be no **communion** whatever between the pure and its opposite.

## CHAPTER VI.

These things also admit of another explanation of the following kind. The <term>theurgist</term> <note>A practitioner of "theurgy" or "god-working," a late-antique ritual system intended to bring the soul into contact with the divine.</note>, through the power of <term>arcane signatures</term> <note>Hidden "tokens" or "marks" placed in the cosmos by the gods; theurgists used these symbols to resonate with divine powers.</note>, commands <term>mundane natures</term> <note>Beings and forces belonging to the physical world, as opposed to the higher, intellectual realms.</note>, no longer as man, nor as employing a human soul; but as existing superior to them in the order of the Gods, he makes use of greater mandates than pertain to himself, so far as he is human. 

This, however, does not take place as if he effected every thing which he vehemently threatens to accomplish; but he teaches us by such a use of words the magnitude and quality of the power which he possesses through a union with the Gods, and which he obtains from the knowledge of <term>arcane symbols</term> <note>Known as "synthemata" in Greek, these were sacred words, stones, or plants used to facilitate divine communication.</note>. 

This, likewise, may be said, that the <term>dæmons</term> <note>In the Platonic tradition, "daemons" were not necessarily evil, but were intermediary spirits who managed the operations of the material world.</note> who are distributed according to parts, and who guard the parts of the universe, pay so much attention to the parts over which they preside, that they cannot endure a word contrary [to the safety of these], but they preserve the permanency of <term>mundane natures</term> immutable. They preserve this permanency, therefore, in an unchanged condition, because the order of the Gods remains invariably the same. Hence they cannot endure even to hear that threatened in which the aerial and terrestrial <term>dæmons</term> have their existence.

<summary>This chapter explains that a theurgist commands cosmic spirits not through human will, but by assuming a divine persona through ritual union with the gods. The "threats" used in rituals are not literal, but serve as displays of authority that lower spirits must obey to maintain the fixed order of the universe.</summary>

## CHAPTER VII.

No one, however, threatens the Gods, nor is such a mode of <term>invocation</term> <note>A formal calling upon a deity or spirit for assistance.</note> addressed to them.

But the Egyptians, mingling <term>dæmoniacal</term> <note>In this context, referring to the "dæmons" or intermediary spirits who handle the mechanics of the material world.</note> words with <term>divine signatures</term> <note>Sacred symbols, sounds, or "passwords" believed to contain the essence of divine power.</note>, sometimes employ threats. 

You have, therefore, an answer to these doubts, concise indeed, but I think sufficiently free from error.

## CHAP. I.

**THE** doubts that follow in the next place also require the assistance of the same divinely-wise Muse for their solution. But before this, I desire to explain to you the unique character of the theology of the Egyptians. For they, imitating the nature of the universe and the <term>fabricative energy</term> <note>The creative, "building" power of the Gods that shapes the physical world.</note> of the Gods, display certain images through symbols of mystic, hidden, and invisible <term>intellections</term> <note>Acts of pure intellectual or spiritual perception; divine thoughts that exist without the need for words.</note>; just as nature, in its own way, expresses invisible principles <note>Literally "reasons" or "logoi"—the underlying rational blueprints of natural things.</note> through visible forms. Indeed, the creative energy of the Gods maps out the truth of forms through these visible images. 

The Egyptians perceived that all superior beings delight in the resemblance that inferior beings bear to them. Because they wished to fill these lower beings with goodness through the greatest possible imitation of the higher ones, they quite properly adopted a method of <term>theologizing</term> <note>The act of discussing, representing, or performing rituals related to the Divine.</note> that is adapted to the secret doctrine hidden within their symbols.

## CHAPTER II.

**LISTEN**, therefore, to the spiritual interpretation of symbols as the Egyptians understood them. At the same time, clear your mind and your ears of the mere physical images of these symbols, and lift yourself up to the intellectual truth. 

By the term **“mire,”** <note>original: "limus". In Neoplatonic thought, mire or mud represents the lowest form of matter—heavy, unstable, and messy—which serves as the "foundation" for physical life.</note> you should understand everything that is physical and material. This includes anything that provides nourishment or is fertile, the various material forms of nature, and everything caught in the ever-changing flux of matter. It refers to the "river" of **generation** <term>generation</term> <note>The constant cycle of birth, growth, and decay in the physical world.</note> and everything that sinks along with it. It also signifies the original cause of the elements and all the powers found within them—a cause that must be understood as the foundation upon which everything else is built. 

Because he is the cause of all life, all nature, and all the powers within the elements, God is superior to all these things. He is immaterial, incorporeal, and supernatural. He is **unbegotten** <note>Existing eternally without having been created or born.</note> and **impartible** <note>Indivisible; a single, unified being that cannot be split into parts.</note>, entirely self-derived and contained within himself. This God precedes all things and holds all things within himself. And because he holds all things and shares himself with all—
