## CHAPTER V.

**You** object, however, “*that he who hears words looks to their signification, so that it is sufficient the conception remains the same, whatever the words may be that are used.*” <note>The author is responding to the "conventionalist" theory of language, which suggests that words are merely arbitrary symbols and that the specific sounds do not matter as long as the idea is communicated.</note> But the thing is not such as you suspect it to be. For if names subsisted through social agreement <term>compact</term> <note>original: "compact." In philosophy, this refers to the idea that language is a human invention created by mutual consent.</note> it would be of no consequence whether some were used instead of others. But if they are suspended from the nature of things, those names which are more adapted to it will also be more dear to the Gods. From this, therefore, it is evident that the language of sacred nations <note>Specifically the Egyptians and Assyrians, who were believed by the Neoplatonists to possess the most ancient and divinely-inspired languages.</note> is very reasonably preferred to that of other men. To which may be added, that names do not entirely preserve the same meaning when translated into another language; but there are certain unique qualities <term>idioms</term> <note>The "idioms" here refer to the intrinsic power and specific nuances of the original sacred tongues that are lost when converted into a more modern or "vulgar" language like Greek or English.</note>

\* See the additional notes at the end of vol. v. of my translation of *Plato*, and also the notes to my translation of Aristotle's *On Interpretation* <note>original: "de Interpretatione"</note>, in which the reader will find a treasury of recondite <note>Recondite: hidden or little-known information.</note> information concerning names, from Proclus and Ammonius. <note>Proclus and Ammonius were later Greek philosophers (Neoplatonists) who wrote extensive commentaries on how language relates to divine reality.</note>

### CHAPTER II

**Prior** to the beings that truly exist and the universal **principles** <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, "principles" are the fundamental sources from which all reality flows.</note> there is one God, prior to the first God and king <note>Referring to a secondary creator-god or "Demiurge" who sits below the ultimate Source.</note>, who remains immoveable, and abiding in the solitude of his **own unity**. They establish the existence of a vital power that existed before the heavens and continues to subsist within them. They also establish a pure intellect above the world, one indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> intellect throughout the whole world, and another intellect which is distributed among all the celestial spheres. They do not examine these things through mere reason alone; rather, through priestly divine-working <note>original: "sacerdotal theurgy"</note>, they announce that they are able to ascend to more elevated and universal essences, and to those powers established above Fate—namely, to God and the Creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note>. In this, they neither employ matter nor rely on anything else, except for the observation of a suitable time.

### CHAPTER V.

# SECTION IX.

## CHAPTER I.

Let us now, therefore, to the utmost of our power, endeavor to discuss the manifold doubts concerning the <term>personal guardian</term> <note>original: "peculiar dæmon" (*idios daimōn*); in Neoplatonic thought, this is a guiding intelligence or spirit assigned to an individual soul to oversee its life and destiny.</note>, a subject which is also prone to various objections. 

To speak summarily, there are two ways to consider the personal guardian: the first is <term>theurgic</term> <note>From the Greek *theourgia* (divine work); refers to rituals designed to connect the practitioner with divine beings and the higher self.</note>, while the other is technical or "artificial." The first method draws this guardian down from <term>higher causes</term> <note>original: "supernal causes"; the spiritual origins and divine principles that exist above the material world.</note>, but the other draws it from the visible cycles of <term>physical life</term> <note>original: "generation"; the constant process of birth, death, and change in the material universe.</note>. One makes no use whatsoever of the calculation of <term>astrological charts</term> <note>original: "nativities"; the practice of determining destiny based on the alignment of the stars at the moment of birth.</note>, while the other meddles with methods of this kind. Furthermore, the one worships this guardian in a way that is more universal and supernatural, while the other is partly aligned with the laws of nature. 

This being the case, you appear to me to have mistakenly applied the principles of a more perfect <term>sacred ritual</term> <note>original: "sacred operation"; a holy practice or divine work intended to elevate the soul.</note> to a merely human system, and it is within this misunderstanding that you have conducted your inquiries.

# CHAPTER II.

Next, it seems to me that you have only addressed a very small portion of the discussion regarding the <term>personal guardian spirit</term> <note>original: "peculiar dæmon" (*idios daimōn*); the specific spiritual guide assigned to an individual soul to oversee its earthly life.</note>. They call upon it by looking to the <term>decans</term> <note>Ten-degree segments of the zodiac (three per sign), each associated with specific powers or deities.</note>, the <term>distributors of cosmic influence</term> <note>original: "dispensators of influxes"; spiritual forces that channel celestial energy down to the material world.</note>, the signs of the zodiac, the stars, the sun and moon, the Great and Little Bear, all the elements, and the world as a whole.

## CHAP. IV.

IF, however, it be necessary, dismissing these particulars, to speak what appears to me to be the truth, you do not rightly infer “*that a knowledge of this <term>mathematical science</term> \* cannot be obtained, because there is much dissonance concerning it, or because Chæremon <note>Chæremon of Alexandria (1st century AD) was an Egyptian priest and Stoic philosopher who wrote on Egyptian religion and astrology.</note>, or some other, has written against it.*” For if this reason were admitted, all things will be incomprehensible. ## CHAPTER IX.

After this, you mention another investigation (<term>disquisition</term> <note>A formal inquiry or systematic search for the truth.</note>) concerning the <term>peculiar dæmon</term> <note>From the Greek *daimōn*; a personal guardian spirit or divine guide assigned to an individual at birth.</note>, which suggests that “*some people worship two, and others three, spirits of this kind.*” However, this entire line of thinking is mistaken. It is a flawed way to proceed to divide the powers that watch over us instead of tracing them back to a single source; such an approach wanders away from the unity that holds authority over all things. 

Similarly, the opinion which splits this spirit into the "body" and the "governance of the body" reduces its divine authority to a very small and insignificant part of our existence. If the very foundation of this belief is so weak, what reason would there be for those who follow it to focus their attention on <term>sacred operations</term> <note>Refers to "theurgy," or rituals intended to invoke the presence of divine beings.</note>? 

Therefore, each of us has one unique, presiding spirit. We should not think that this spirit is a single entity common to all humanity; nor should we think it is a universal force that just happens to be present in each individual. Differences in physical matter and individual species do not allow for the same kind of shared participation (<term>communion</term>) found in things that are essentially <term>incorporeal</term> <note>Existing without a physical or material body; purely spiritual.</note>.

“*Why then,*” [you ask,] “*is the personal spirit called upon by a common method by all men?*” It is because the act of calling upon him is carried out through a single...

## CHAPTER III

## CHAPTER V.

**BUT** why am I speaking at such length about these details? For I have already shown enough, in what has been said before, the superiority of divine prophecy over human <term>divination</term> <note>The practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown through communication with the divine.</note>. It is better, therefore, in answering your request, "*to point out to you the way to happiness, and show you what its essence consists of.*" For from this the truth will be discovered, and at the same time all doubts may be easily resolved. I say, therefore, that the more divine <note>original: θεωτερος (theioteros), meaning "more divine." The translator notes a correction from the original Greek text θεῶτος (theotos).</note> <term>intelligible man</term> <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to the eternal, spiritual essence of a human being that exists in the realm of pure thought (the Intellect) before descending into a physical body.</note>, who was formerly united to the Gods by the vision of them, afterwards entered into another soul, which is fitted to the human form, and through this became bound with the chains of necessity and fate. Hence it is necessary to consider how he may be set free from these bonds. *There is, therefore, no other way to break them than the knowledge of the Gods.* For to know <term>the Good</term> <note>The supreme principle in Platonic philosophy, representing the ultimate source of all truth, beauty, and existence.</note> through true science is the very form of <term>felicity</term> <note>A state of supreme happiness or spiritual blessedness; the ultimate goal of human life.</note>; just as the forgetting of the good, and deception about evil, happen to be the very form of evil. The former, therefore, is present with the divine; but the latter, which is a lower destiny, is inseparable from our mortal nature.

# CHAPTER VII.

**WITH** respect to *the good*, likewise, they <note>Referring to the Egyptian priests and sages mentioned in the preceding chapters.</note> conceive that one kind is divine, and this is the God who is prior to the <term>intelligible</term> <note>The "intelligible" realm refers to the highest level of reality that can be grasped by the mind or intellect, beyond the physical world of the senses.</note>; but that the other is human, and is a union with the former. And these two kinds of good <term>Bitys</term> <note>A legendary Egyptian figure, often identified as a priest or prophet who interpreted the secret teachings of Hermes for the Egyptian kings.</note> has unfolded from the <term>Hermaic</term> <note>Related to Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of Egyptian wisdom, writing, and magic, often identified with the god Thoth.</note> books. This part, therefore, is not, as you suspect, omitted by the Egyptians, but is divinely delivered by them. Nor do “*theurgists disturb the divine intellect about trifling concerns;*” but they consult it about things which pertain to the purification, liberation, and salvation of the soul. Neither do they studiously employ themselves in things which are indeed difficult, yet useless to mankind; but, on the contrary, they direct their attention to things which are of all others most beneficial to the soul. Nor, in the last place, are “*they deceived by a certain fraudulent <term>dæmon</term>,*” <note>From the Greek "daimon." In this context, it refers to a spiritual or intermediary being. The text argues that the ritual specialist (theurgist) is not being tricked by low-level spirits but is reaching for the divine.</note> who, having vanquished a fallacious and dæmoniacal nature, ascend to an intelligible and divine essence.

## CHAPTER VIII.

**AND** thus we have answered, to the utmost of our ability, your inquiries concerning **divination** <term>divination</term> <note>The practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the hidden will of the gods through ritual or inspiration.</note> and **theurgy** <term>theurgy</term> <note>Literally "god-working." Unlike mere sorcery, theurgy was a high religious practice aimed at purifying the soul and uniting it with the divine through sacred rituals.</note>. It remains, therefore, at the end of this discussion, that I should beseech the **Gods** to afford me an immutable guard of **true conceptions** <note>In this Neoplatonic context, these are clear, unchanging intellectual understandings of reality, as opposed to the shifting opinions of the material world.</note>, to insert in me **truth** eternally, and to supply me abundantly with the participation of more perfect **conceptions of the Gods**, in which the most blessed end of our good is posited <note>The "end" or *telos* refers to the ultimate goal of human life—union with the divine.</note>, and the confirmation of our concordant friendship with each other.

**Page 9.** *Anebo*. Porphyry <note>A prominent Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) and student of Plotinus; he wrote a letter to the Egyptian priest Anebo questioning the validity of certain religious practices.</note> in his *Life of Plotinus*, and also in the second book of his *Treatise on Abstinence from Animals*, informs us that he was familiar with a certain Egyptian priest, who, as the scholar Gale conjectures, is probably the priest to whom Porphyry now writes. The style of writing, indeed, as Gale observes, indicates that the person to whom this letter is addressed was a very **great prophet**, who, nevertheless, is afterwards called a **priest**. This, however, is not anything new or out of place. For according to Apuleius in the *Metamorphoses*, book 11, the Egyptian Zaclas is said to be a **chief prophet and priest** <note>original Latin: "propheta primarius et sacerdos"</note>.

**Page 9.** *Hermes the God who presides over language*. The Egyptians celebrated two versions of Hermes, the first of which is referred to here by Iamblichus. This deity is the source of **invention**, and for this reason, he is said to be the son of **Maia**; because **search** (which is implied by the name Maia) leads **invention** into the light. He also grants **learning** <term>mathesis</term> <note>From the Greek word for "study" or "knowledge"; here it refers to the spiritual and intellectual discipline of the soul.</note> to souls by revealing the will of his father Jupiter; he does this as the angel or messenger of Jupiter. The philosopher Proclus, in a manuscript commentary on Plato's *Alcibiades*, observes "that this deity is the respective guardian of **gymnastic exercises**; and for this reason, **statues of Hermes** <term>hermæ</term> <note>Square stone pillars topped with a bust, often of Hermes, which served as boundary markers and decorations in athletic spaces.</note> were placed in the **wrestling schools** <term>Palæstræ</term> <note>Ancient Greek buildings dedicated to the training of wrestlers and other athletes.</note>; he also guards **music**, and is therefore honored as the **lyre-player** <note>original Greek: λυραιος (luraios)</note> among the stars; and he guards **disciplines**, because the invention of geometry, reasoning, and speech is attributed to this God. He presides, therefore, over every kind of education, leading us toward a **divine reality** <note>referred to as "intelligible essence"—the realm of pure, unchanging truth beyond the physical world</note> from this mortal home, governing the different groups of souls, and clearing away the sleep and forgetfulness that weigh them down. He is likewise the provider of memory, the goal of which is a true intellectual understanding of divine natures."

**P. 15.** *There is, therefore, the good itself which is beyond essence, and there is that good which subsists according to essence.* There are three orders of good; namely, that which is <term>imparticipable</term> <note>Something that exists in its own right and is not shared or "participated in" by lower things; a pure, transcendent source.</note> and <term>superessential</term> <note>Existing beyond the realm of "being" or "essence"; the highest possible state in Neoplatonic thought.</note>; that which is imparticipable and essential; and that which is essential and <term>participable</term> <note>A quality or essence that can be shared by or present within multiple individual things.</note>. Of these, the last is such as our nature contains; **the good** which ranks among forms is essential; and that which is beyond essence is superessential. 

Or we say that **the good** which subsists in us may be considered as a habit, in consequence of subsisting in a subject; the next to this ranks as essence, and a part of essence—I mean **the good** which ranks among forms; and **the good** which is beyond essence, is neither a habit, nor a part. 

With respect to **the good**, also, which subsists according to essence, it must be observed, that since forms are twofold—some alone distinguishing the **essences** of the things fashioned by form, but others their **perfections**—the genus of essence, same and different, and the form of animal, horse, and man, and every thing of this kind, give distinction to essence and subjects; but the form of **the good**, the beautiful, and the just, and in like manner the form of virtue, of health, strength, and every thing of a similar nature, are perfective of the beings to which they belong: and of some, essence is the leader, but of others **the good**. 

For, as Plato says, every thing except **the one**, must necessarily participate of essence; and whatever preserves, gives perfection to, or defends any being, must be good. Hence, since these two are leaders, the one of forms which give subsistence to things, and the other of such as are the sources of their perfection; it is necessary that one of these should be subordinate to the other; I mean that **the good** which is allotted a coordination among forms that are the sources of perfection, should be subordinate to essence, which ranks among causes, whence subsistence originates, if **the good** is being, and a certain being. For it is either the same with, or different from, essence, which the Elean guest <note>A character in Plato's dialogues, often representing a more advanced philosophical perspective than the earlier Socratic figures.</note> or stranger in the ***Sophist*** <note>original Latin: "Sophista"; one of Plato's dialogues concerning the nature of being and non-being.</note> of Plato shows to be the genus of being. And if **the good** is the same with...

**P. 22. *One and the best solution will be obtained by surveying the mode of divine allotment.***

The manner in which <term>divine allotments</term> <note>The way the gods distribute their influence or "assign" portions of the universe to be under their care.</note> subsist is admirably unfolded by <term>Proclus</term> <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher (5th century AD) who sought to synthesize all of Greek philosophy into a single system.</note> in his commentary on the *Timaeus*, page 43, as follows:

"Since, according to a division of the universe into two parts, we have distributed allotments into the celestial and sublunary <note>The region "below the moon," meaning the Earth and its atmosphere, characterized by change and decay.</note>, there can be no doubt what the former are, and whether they possess an invariable sameness of subsistence. But the sublunary allotments are deservedly a subject of admiration, whether they are said to be perpetual or not. For since all things in <term>generation</term> <note>The physical world of birth, death, and constant change.</note> are continually changing and flowing, how can the allotments of the providential rulers of them be said to be perpetual? For things in generation are not perpetual. But if their allotments are not perpetual, how is it possible to suppose that divine government can subsist differently at different times? For an allotment is neither a certain separate energy of the Gods—so that even if sublunary natures were changing, we might say that the divine energy is exempt and remains immutable—nor is it that which is governed alone, so that no absurdity would follow from admitting that an allotment is in a flowing condition, and is conversant with all various mutations; but it is a providential inspection, and unrestrained government of divinity over sublunary concerns. Such being the doubts with which this subject is attended, the following appears to be a solution of the difficulty.

"We must say, then, that it is not proper to consider all the natures that are in generation, and generation itself, as alone consisting of things mutable and flowing, but that there is also something immutable in these, and which is naturally adapted to remain perpetually the same. For the <term>interval</term> <note>Space or the cosmic "receptacle" that holds the physical world.</note> which receives and comprehends in itself all the parts of the world, and which has an arrangement through all bodies, is immoveable, lest, being moved, it should require another place, and thus should proceed from one receptacle to another, *to infinity* <note>original: "ad infinitum"</note>. The etherial vehicles, also, of divine souls, with which they are circularly invested, and which imitate the lives in the heavens, have a perpetual...

Proclus argues that even in our world of "generation," there are immutable structures like space and the ethereal bodies of souls that allow for permanent divine governance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of how divine influence reaches the earth. ...fabricated a <term>sacred science</term> <note>This refers to theurgy, a type of ritual practice where humans attempt to communicate or unite with the divine through the natural world.</note> from this mutual sympathy and similarity. Thus they recognised things supreme in such as are subordinate, and the subordinate in the supreme: in the celestial regions, <term>terrene</term> <note>Meaning "earthly" or belonging to the world of matter.</note> properties subsisting in a causal and celestial manner; and in earth celestial properties, but according to a terrene condition. For how shall we account for those plants called <term>heliotropes</term> <note>From the Greek 'helios' (sun) and 'trepo' (to turn); plants like the sunflower that follow the sun's path.</note>, that is, attendants on the sun, moving in correspondence with the revolution of its orb, but <term>selenitropes</term> <note>From the Greek 'selene' (moon); plants believed to follow the phases or movement of the moon.</note>, or attendants on the moon, turning in exact conformity to her motion? It is because all things pray, and hymn the leaders of their respective orders; but some intellectually, and others rationally; some in a natural, and others after a sensible, manner. 

Hence the sunflower, as far as it is able, moves in a circular dance towards the sun; so that if any one could hear the pulsation made by its circuit in the air, he would perceive something composed by a sound of this kind, in honour of its king, such as a plant is capable of framing. Hence, too, we may behold the sun and moon in the earth, but according to a terrene quality; but in the celestial regions, all plants, and stones, and animals, possessing an intellectual life according to a celestial nature. Now the ancients, having contemplated this mutual sympathy of things, applied for <term>occult</term> <note>In this context, 'occult' means 'hidden' or 'secret'—referring to the unseen forces of nature.</note> purposes, both celestial and terrene natures, by means of which, through a certain similitude, they deduced <term>divine virtues</term> <note>The specific powers or spiritual energies belonging to the Gods.</note> into this inferior abode. 

For, indeed, similitude itself is a sufficient cause of binding things together in union and consent. Thus, if a piece of paper is heated, and afterwards placed near a lamp, though it does not touch the fire, the paper will be suddenly inflamed, and the flame will descend from the superior to the inferior parts. This heated paper we may compare to a certain relation of inferiors to superiors; and its approximation to the lamp, to the opportune use of things according to time, place, and matter. But the <term>procession</term> <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, this is the way divine energy flows outward and downward from the source into the material world.</note> of fire into the paper, aptly represents the presence of divine light to that nature which is capable of its reception. Lastly, the inflammation of the paper may be compared to the <term>deification</term> <note>The process of a mortal or material thing becoming divine or being filled with a God's presence.</note> of mortals, and to the illumination of material natures, which are afterwards carried upwards, like the enkindled paper, from a certain participation of <term>divine seed</term> <note>The spark of divinity or creative principle inherent in all things.</note>.

Besides this, they collected composite odours, by a divine art, into one, comprehending a multitude of powers, and symbolizing with the unity of a divine essence; considering that division debilitates each of these, but that mingling them together restores them to the idea of their exemplar.

P. 35. *Since, however, the order of all the Gods is profoundly united.——For the very existence in them, whatever it may be, is the one of their nature.*

The Gods are **superessential unities** <term>superessential</term> <note>Existing beyond "essence" or "being." This describes a level of reality higher than anything that can be defined or categorized by human thought.</note>, so far as they are Gods. For the principal subsistence of every thing is according to the summit of its essence, and this in the Gods is *the one*, through which they are profoundly united to each other and to **the one itself** <term>The One</term> <note>The ultimate, absolute principle in Neoplatonism; the source from which all reality flows.</note>, or the ineffable principle of things, from which they are ineffably unfolded into light. Concerning this union of them with each other, **Proclus** <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was one of the last major Greek philosophers; he headed the Platonic Academy in Athens and systematized Neoplatonic thought.</note> admirably observes as follows, in his manuscript Commentary on the *Parmenides* of Plato <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the nature of "The One" and the "Many," which Proclus used to explain the structure of the divine hierarchy.</note>. “All these **unities** <term>unities</term> <note>Also called "henads," these are the individual gods seen as pure expressions of unity before they manifest as specific powers or beings.</note> are in, and are profoundly united to, each other, and their union is far greater than the communion and sameness which subsist in beings. For in the latter there is indeed a mutual mixture of forms, similitude, and friendship, and a participation of each other; but the union of the Gods, as being a union of unities, is much more uniform, ineffable, and transcendent: for here *all* are *in all*, which does not take place in forms or ideas; \* and their unmingled purity, and the characteristic of each, in a manner far surpassing the diversity in ideas, preserves their natures unconfused, and distinguishes their peculiar powers. Hence, some of them are more universal, and others more particular; some of them are characterised by **permanency**, others by **progression**, and others by **conversion**, or regression <note>The three stages of Neoplatonic emanation: staying (remaining in the source), moving out (creation), and returning (the soul's journey back to the divine).</note>. Some, again, are generative, others **anagogic** <term>anagogic</term> <note>From the Greek word for "leading upward"; refers to powers that help the soul ascend back to the divine world.</note>, or of an elevating nature,

---

\* For in these, all are in each, but not all in all.

> "Indeed we obtain this knowledge of their union and characteristics from the natures by which they are participated. For, with respect to the visible Gods <note>The "visible Gods" refers to the stars and planets, which Neoplatonists believed were the physical bodies of divine beings.</note>, we say that there is one soul of the sun, and another of the earth, directing our attention to the visible bodies of these divinities, which possess much variety in their essence, power, and dignity among wholes. As, therefore, we apprehend the difference of incorporeal essences from sensible inspection <note>That is, observing the physical world helps us understand the spiritual world.</note>, in like manner from the variety of incorporeal essences we are enabled to know something of the unmingled distinction of the first and <term>superessential unities</term> <note>Terms describing the "Henads," or the most fundamental gods who exist even beyond the level of "Being" or "Essence."</note>, and of the characteristics of each. And thus far does the progression of the unities extend." Shortly after he adds, "As trees by their extremities are rooted in the earth, and through this are earthly in every part, in the same manner divine natures are rooted by their summits in *the one*, and each is a *unity* and *one*, through its unconfused union with *the one itself*." ->**Like Mars, when brandishing his spear, he raged.** <note>original: "ὁ δ’ ἐμαίνετο, ὡς ὅτ’ ’Άρης ἐγχέσπαλος" — *Iliad* xv. 605. This describes Hector’s battle-fury as being like that of the god of war.</note><-

But if someone, giving in to a craving, should eat something that reason forbids, and through this should unexpectedly recover their health, you might say that the craving also, in this instance, acted with a kind of inspired energy, though in a hidden way; thus, a form of inspiration can occur in the other, lower parts of the soul as well. 

However, "enthusiasm" <note>In the Greek sense of *enthousiasmos*, meaning to be "filled with the god."</note> in its truest sense is when this <term>one of the soul</term> <note>The highest, most unified part of the human spirit, which sits above the intellect and is capable of touching the Divine.</note>, which is above the intellect, is awakened toward the Gods and is inspired by them. At different times, the soul is possessed by different Gods depending on its own readiness; and it is more or less possessed when the intellect or the <term>dianoia</term> <note>The faculty of discursive reasoning or step-by-step logical thinking.</note> is the part being moved. 

Just as we do not always define "philosophy" with total precision—often using the word loosely to refer to mathematics or physics—we do the same with "enthusiasm." For even if it is only the <term>phantasy</term> <note>The faculty of imagination or mental imagery.</note> that is excited, we are accustomed to calling that excitement "enthusiasm." 

Furthermore, those who claim that enthusiasm comes from the physical temperature of bodies, the quality of the air, the rising of vapors, the suitability of certain times and places, or the movement of the stars, are speaking only of the supporting and material causes of the experience, rather than its true, primary causes. 

To summarize the causes of divine inspiration:
*   The **producing cause** is the Gods.
*   The **material cause** is the inspired soul itself, or the external sacred symbols used.
*   The **formal cause** is the divine inspiration itself acting upon *the one of the soul*.
*   The **final cause** is the achievement of the Good.

"If, however, the Gods always wish for the soul’s good, why does the soul not always act with divine inspiration?" We might say that while the Gods always wish for the soul’s good, they also intend for the order of the entire universe to be maintained. Because of many different factors, the soul is not always prepared or "tuned" for inspiration, and for this reason, it does not always act with that divine energy. 

Some suggest that the <term>telestic art</term> <note>The "art of the mysteries" or theurgy; the practice of rituals intended to draw the soul toward the divine.</note> only reaches as far as the <term>sublunary region</term> <note>The realm of the four elements (Earth, Water, Air, Fire) located below the moon, characterized by change and decay.</note>. If they mean that none of the <term>superlunary</term> <note>The celestial realm of the stars and planets, considered eternal and unchanging.</note> or heavenly beings act within the sublunary realm, they are clearly making an absurd claim.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on "enthusiasm" (divine inspiration) and the limits of the soul's power. It follows the previous page’s distinction between true divine possession—which happens in the highest part of the soul—and lower forms of inspiration or natural impulses.</meta>

<page-num>353</page-num>

But if they claim that the <term>Telestæ</term> <note>From the Greek *telestai*, meaning "mystic operators" or theurgists—priests who performed sacred rituals to connect the human with the divine.</note>, or mystic operators, are not able to act with divine power above the lunar sphere, we respond that if every soul's assigned place was only beneath the moon, their claim would be true. However, there are also assignments for souls above the moon (for some are followers of the sun, others of the moon, and others of Saturn, since the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>The "Divine Craftsman" or creator-god who shaped the material universe.</note> scattered some into the earth, others into the moon, and others elsewhere). This being the case, it is indeed possible for the soul to act above the moon. For whatever the entire cosmic order grants to the soul over a very long period of time, the soul is also able to grant to itself for a short duration when it is assisted by the Gods through the <term>telestic art</term> <note>The practice of theurgy, or sacred ritual, intended to purify the soul and draw down divine influence.</note>. The soul can never act beyond the limits of its own assigned nature, but it can act to the very edge of those limits. For example, if a soul’s natural limit reached as far as philosophy, even if that soul did not choose a philosophical life but some other path, it would still be able to act somewhat philosophically within that other life. There are also said to be certain <term>supermundane</term> <note>Existing "above the world" or beyond the physical universe.</note> souls. And so, we have shown how the soul acts with divine inspiration.

But how can statues be said to possess this "inspired energy"? We might say that a statue, being lifeless, does not itself act toward divinity. Instead, the telestic art purifies the matter the statue is made of and places sacred <term>characters and symbols</term> <note>Mystical marks (*charaktêres*) or ritual tokens (*synthêmata*) believed to resonate with divine powers.</note> around it. First, through these means, the art makes the statue "animated"—giving it a kind of life drawn from the world—and then it prepares the statue to be illuminated by a divine nature. Through this divine light, the statue delivers oracles for as long as it remains properly fit to receive it. Once the statue has been made perfect by this sacred art, it remains [endued with a prophetic power] until it becomes entirely unfit for divine light. 

A human who receives the inspiring influence of the Gods, however, only receives it at certain times, not constantly. This is because the soul, when filled with the deity, acts through that power; because it is acting above its own natural strength, it eventually becomes exhausted. Indeed, the soul would be a God itself—and similar to the souls of the stars—if it never grew weary. But the statue remains illuminated according to how it was prepared to participate in that power. Therefore, its loss of power only happens if it falls into a state of total emptiness, unless it is again, *anew* <note>original: "de novo"</note>, made perfect and given life by the mystic operator. We have sufficiently shown, therefore, that enthusiasm, properly so called, takes place within the <term>one of the soul</term> <note>The "flower" or highest point of the spirit that is capable of direct union with the Divine.</note>, and that it is a light shining from the divinity.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of divine inspiration (enthusiasm) from page 353, shifting from the general possibility of the soul's ascent to the specific "four manias" described by Plato in the *Phaedrus*.</meta>

Next, let us discuss the order and the use of the four <term>manias</term> <note>From the Greek *mania*, meaning "madness." In Platonic philosophy, this refers not to mental illness, but to "divine madness"—a state of inspired possession that elevates the human soul toward the divine.</note>, and show why the philosopher <note>Plato.</note> mentions only these. Is it because there are no others besides these, or because these were sufficient for his purpose?

Plato himself indicates as he proceeds that there are many other divine inspirations and manias, and before this, he mentions the inspiration that comes from the Nymphs. There are also inspirations from Pan, from the Mother of the Gods <note>Cybele, the Phrygian mother goddess.</note>, and from the <term>Corybantes</term> <note>Armed and music-making worshippers of the Great Mother, known for their ecstatic rites.</note>, which are mentioned by Plato elsewhere. 

Here, however, he only presents these four manias; first, because these alone are sufficient for the soul to achieve its proper <term>apocatastasis</term> <note>A Greek term meaning "restoration" or "return," referring to the soul's journey back to its original, perfect divine state.</note>, as we shall show later; and secondly, because he is describing the immediate steps of the soul's ascent. 

The gifts of the Gods to all beings are many and beyond human understanding. But here, he is describing the specific activities of the Gods that are extended to souls. He presents these four manias not because any one of them—especially the <term>amatory</term> <note>The "madness" of love (Eros), which leads the soul to the contemplation of Beauty itself.</note>—would not be enough to lead the soul back to its original happiness, but because he is unfolding the entire sequence, the regular gradation, and the orderly perfection of the soul.

Just as it is possible for a <term>tyrannic life</term> <note>A reference to the political hierarchy in Plato’s *Republic*, where the tyrant represents the lowest, most disordered state of the soul.</note> to be suddenly changed and become <term>aristocratic</term> <note>The "best" life, ruled by reason and virtue.</note> through intense readiness and a divine gift, the gradual ascent usually moves from a tyrannic to a democratic life, then to an oligarchic one, then to a <term>timocratic</term> <note>A society or soul-state based on honor and ambition.</note>, and finally to an aristocratic life—while the descent and fall happen in the opposite order. 

In the same way, when the soul is about to ascend and be restored to its former happiness, it is possessed:
1. First, by the **musical mania**.
2. Second, by the **telestic mania** <note>The inspiration of the sacred rites or "mystic operators."</note>.
3. Third, by the **prophetic mania**.
4. And finally, by the **amatory mania**.

These inspirations, however, work together and need one another, so great is their connection. For the <term>telestic</term> requires the <term>prophetic</term> <note>original Greek: *mantikes*. The source text corrected this from "musical."</note> mania, since prophecy interprets many things belonging to the sacred rituals. And again, the prophetic requires the telestic mania, because the telestic mania perfects and establishes the truth of oracular predictions. 

Furthermore, the prophetic uses the poetic and musical mania, for prophets, as I might say, always speak in verse. And again, the musical uses the prophetic mania spontaneously, as Plato says. But what need is there to speak further about the amatory and musical—

> “ It remains, therefore, that we should unfold the nature of each of the manias, previously observing that those which are internal, and originate from the soul itself, and give perfection to it, are of one kind; but the external energies of them, and which preserve the outward man, and our nature, are of another. The four external, however, are analogous to the four internal manias. Let us consider, therefore, in the first place, the internal, and which alone originate from the soul itself, and let us see what they effect in the soul. In order, likewise, that this may become manifest, and also their arrangement, let us survey from on high, the descent, as Plato says, and defluxion of the wings of the soul. From the beginning, therefore, and at first, the soul was united to the Gods, and its unity to their one <note>The Neoplatonic concept of the "One," the ultimate source of all existence.</note>. But afterwards the soul departing from this divine union descended into intellect, and no longer possessed real beings unitedly, and in one, but apprehended and surveyed them by simple projections, and, as it were, contacts of its intellect. In the next place, departing from intellect, and descending into reasoning and <term>dianoia</term> <note>From the Greek *dianoia*, meaning "discursive reasoning"—the type of step-by-step logical thinking used in mathematics and philosophy, as opposed to direct intellectual intuition.</note>, it no longer apprehended real beings by simple intuitions, but syllogistically and transitively, proceeding from one thing to another, from propositions to conclusions. Afterwards, abandoning true reasoning, and the dissolving peculiarity, it descended into generation <note>The realm of physical birth, change, and decay.</note>, and became filled with much irrationality and perturbation. to its proper principles and again return to the place from whence it came. To this ascent and <term>apocatastasis</term> <note>The restoration of the soul to its original, divine state of being.</note>, however, these four manias contribute. And the musical mania, indeed, leads to symphony and harmony, the agitated and disturbed nature of the parts of the soul, which were hurried away to indefiniteness and inaptitude, and were filled with abundant tumult. But the <term>telestic mania</term> <note>The inspiration related to sacred rites and initiations (from the Greek "telestike").</note> causes the soul to be perfect and entire, and prepares it to energize intellectually. For the musical mania alone harmonizes and represses the parts of the soul; but the telestic causes the whole of it to energize, and prepares it to become entire, so that the intellectual part of it may energize. For the soul, by descending into the realms of <term>generation</term> <note>The physical world of birth, death, and constant change.</note>, resembles a thing broken and relaxed. And the **circle of the same**, or the intellectual part of it, is fettered; but the **circle of the different**, or the <term>doxastic part</term> <note>The part of the soul dealing with "doxa" (opinion and sensory perception) rather than absolute truth.</note>, sustains many fractures and turnings. <note>These "circles" refer to the structure of the soul as described in Plato's *Timaeus*, where the soul is composed of a movement of Sameness (reason) and a movement of Difference (opinion).</note> Hence, the soul energizes partially, and not according to the whole of itself. The **Dionysiacal** inspiration, therefore, after the parts of the soul are coharmonized, renders it perfect, and causes it to energize according to the whole of itself, and to live intellectually. But the **Apolloniacal** mania converts and coexcites all the multiplied powers, and the whole of the soul, to *the one* of it. Hence Apollo is denominated as elevating the soul from multitude to *the one*. And the remaining mania, the **amatory**, receiving the soul united, conjoins this one of the soul to the Gods, and to intelligible beauty. As the givers, therefore, of these manias are transcendently united, and are in each other, the gifts also on this account participate of, and communicate with, each other, and the recipient, which is the soul, possesses an adaptation to all the gifts. This, therefore, is the order, and these are the energies and powers within the soul itself, of these four manias.

“ But let us also consider their external energies on man, and what they outwardly effect about us. The musical mania, therefore, causes us to speak in verse, and to act and be moved rythmically, and to sing in metre, the splendid deeds of divine men, and their virtues and pursuits; and, through these, to discipline our life, in the same manner as the inward manias coharmonize our soul. But the telestic mania, expelling every thing foreign, contaminating, and noxious, preserves our life perfect and innoxious, and banishing an insane and diabolical <term>phantasy</term> <note>In ancient philosophy, this refers to the "imagination" or "mental images" that can lead the mind astray if not purified.</note>, causes us to be sane, entire, and perfect, just as the internal telestic mania makes the soul to be perfect and entire. [Pro]phetic mania <note>The inspiration of Apollo, which grants foresight.</note> contracts into one the extension and infinity of time, and sees, as in one present *now*, all things: the past, the future, and the existing time. Hence it predicts what will be, which it sees as present to itself. It causes us, therefore, to pass through life in an irreprehensible manner, just as the internal prophetic mania contracts and elevates all the multiplied and many powers and lives of the soul to the **one**, in order that it may in a greater degree be preserved and connected. But the amatory mania <note>The inspiration of Love (Eros), which directs the soul toward beauty.</note> converts young persons to us, and causes them to become our friends, being instructive of youth, and leading them from sensible beauty <note>Beauty that can be perceived by the five senses.</note> to our psychical beauty <note>The beauty of the soul and character.</note>, and from this sending them to intelligible beauty <note>The ultimate, divine form of Beauty that exists beyond the physical world.</note>; in the same manner as the internal amatory mania conjoins the **one** of the soul to the Gods.

> "All the above mentioned manias, therefore, are superior to the prudent and temperate energies of the soul. For certain inspirations are produced according to the middle and also according to the <term>doxastic reasons</term> <note>The "doxastic" part of the soul is responsible for "doxa" (opinion or belief), sitting between raw sensory perception and pure intellectual understanding.</note> of the soul, conformably to which artists effect certain things, and discover theorems beyond expectation, as Asclepius <note>The Greek god of medicine and healing.</note>, for instance, in medicine, and Hercules in the <term>practic life</term> <note>The "active" or "practical" life of moral action and physical labor, as opposed to the "theoretical" or "contemplative" life.</note>."

Afterwards, in commenting on what Plato says of the mania from the Muses, viz. But Plato says, "that he who without the divinely-inspired mania of the Muses expects to become a divine poet, will, by thus fancying, become himself imperfect, and his poetry will be vanquished and concealed by the poetry which is the progeny of mania." Hermeas adds, "For what similitude is there between the poetry of Chærilus and Callimachus, and that of Homer and Pindar? For the divinely-inspired poets, as being filled

Which reminds me of what Suetonius relates of Caligula, that he would place himself between the statues of Castor and Pollux, and confer privately with Jupiter Capitolinus, fancying that he was intimate with, and of equal dignity with these divinities. And as to the poets that have lived since the fall of the Roman empire, it would be ridiculous to suppose that they possessed this highest enthusiasm <note>original: "enthusiasm" here refers to divine inspiration or "theos," the state of being filled with a god</note>, as they did not believe in the existence of the sources from which it is alone genuinely derived.

**Page 67. *The attentive power of the soul.*** This is that act or power of the rational soul which primarily apprehends the operations of the senses. For the rational soul not only has intellect in capacity, the dianoetic power <note>original: "dianoetic" refers to the power of discursive reasoning or logical thought</note>, will, and choice, but another power, which is called by the best of Greek interpreters of Aristotle, as well as by Iamblichus, *prosektikon* <note>original: προσϵκτικον</note>, *the attentive*. This power investigates and perceives whatever is transacted in man; and says, "I understand, I think, I opine, I am angry, I desire." And in short, this attentive part of the rational soul passes through the rational, irrational, vegetable, or physical powers. Since, therefore, it is requisite it should pass through all these powers, it will also proceed through the senses, and shall say, "I see, I hear"; for it is the peculiarity of that which apprehends energies thus to speak. Hence if it is the attentive power which says these things, it is this power which apprehends the energy of sensibles <note>original: "sensibles" refers to things perceived by the senses</note>; for it is necessary that the nature which apprehends all things should be one, since man also is one. For if one part of it should apprehend *these*, and another *those* things, it is just, as Aristotle says, as if you should perceive *this* thing, and *I* that. It is necessary, therefore, that the attentive power should be an indivisible thing.

**Page 74. *For the human soul is on all sides darkened by the body, which he who denominates the river of Negligence, the water of Oblivion, etc.***—will not by such appellation sufficiently express its turpitude <note>original: "turpitude" here refers to the inherent baseness or corruption of the material state</note>.

> "The whole of generation <note>original: "generation" refers to the realm of physical birth and material existence</note>, as well as the human body," says Proclus in his fifth book, page 339, "may be called a river, through its rapid, impetuous, and unstable flux. Thus also in the *Republic*, Plato calls the whole genesiurgic <note>original: "genesiurgic" refers to the power or realm that produces physical life</note> nature the river of Lethe <note>original: "Lethē," the river of forgetfulness in Greek mythology</note>, in which are contained, as Empedocles says, Oblivion and the meadow of Ate <note>original: "Ate" refers to a state of delusion or ruin</note>; the voracity of matter, and the light-hating world, as the Gods say; and the winding streams."

P. 105. *But there are a certain few who by employing a certain supernatural power of intellect, are removed from nature, &c.* The class to which these few belong is beautifully unfolded, as follows, by <term>Plotinus</term> <note>A philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) who is regarded as the father of Neoplatonism, a school of thought emphasizing the soul's ascent to "the One."</note>, in the beginning of his Treatise on <term>Intellect</term>, <term>Ideas</term>, and <term>real Being</term>. 

> “Since all men from their birth employ sense prior to intellect, and are necessarily first conversant with <term>sensibles</term> <note>Things that can be perceived by the five senses, such as physical objects.</note>, some proceeding no farther, pass through life, considering these as the first and last of things, and apprehending that whatever is painful among these is evil, and whatever is pleasant is good; thus thinking it sufficient to pursue the one and avoid the other. Those, too, among them who pretend to a greater share of reason than others, esteem this to be wisdom, being affected in a manner similar to more heavy birds, who collecting many things from the earth, and being oppressed with the weight, are unable to fly on high, though they have received wings for this purpose from nature. But others are in a small degree elevated from things subordinate, the more excellent part of the soul recalling them from pleasure to a more worthy pursuit. As they are, however, unable to look on high, and as not possessing any thing else which can afford them rest, they betake themselves, together with the name of virtue, to actions and the election of things inferior, from which they at first endeavoured to raise themselves, though in vain. *In the third class is the race of divine men*, who, through a more excellent power, and with piercing eyes, acutely perceive supernal light, to the vision of which they raise themselves above the clouds and darkness, as it were, of this lower world, and there abiding despise every thing in these regions of sense; being no otherwise delighted with the place which is truly and properly their own, than he who after many wanderings is at length restored to his lawful country.”

P. 123. *And such as have written concerning the decans.* The twelve parts, mentioned in the preceding chapter, into which the Egyptians divide the heavens, are the twelve signs of the zodiac. But the thirty-six parts are the twelve houses of the planets, divided into three other portions, which they call **decans** <note>From the Greek word for "ten"; these are 36 groups of stars (constellations) used in Ancient Egyptian astronomy to divide the 360-degree zodiac into 10-degree segments.</note>. Ptolemy, however, in his *Quadripartite* <note>original: "Quadripartite"; referring to Ptolemy’s famous astrological work, the Tetrabiblos.</note>, subverts this doctrine of the Egyptians. Concerning these decans, see Scaliger on Manilius <note>original: "Scaliger ad Manilium"; referring to Joseph Justus Scaliger’s commentary on the Roman astronomical poet Manilius.</note>, Kircher in the second part of *Oedipus* <note>original: "Kircher ii. parte Oedipi"; referring to Athanasius Kircher’s "Oedipus Aegyptiacus," a massive 17th-century study of Egyptian lore.</note>, and Salmasius *On Climacteric Years* <note>original: "Salmasius de Annis climactericis"; a work by Claude Saumaise regarding critical years in a person's life based on astrology.</note>. Gale also gives the following extract from Hermes relative to the decans, which had not been before published, and which he derived from a manuscript copy of Stobæus in the possession of Vossius.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on the nature of the divine and the structure of the cosmos, moving from the primary principles (the One and Being) discussed on page 362 to the celestial guardians known as decans and the philosophical interpretation of divine "flexibility" in prayer.</meta>

<page-num>363</page-num>

“We say, O son, that the body [of the universe] is comprehensive of all things. Conceive of it, therefore, as being like a circular form—and understand that under the circle of this body the thirty-six <term>decans</term> <note>The decans are 36 groups of stars used in ancient Egyptian astronomy to mark time; in this philosophical context, they are viewed as celestial powers that maintain cosmic order.</note> are arranged, in the middle of the whole circle of the zodiac. Let us understand them as if they were guardians presiding over everything in the world, holding all things together and preserving the established order of all things. Furthermore, understand, O <term>Tat</term> <note>In Hermetic writings, Tat is the son and student of the legendary sage Hermes Trismegistus.</note>, that these decans are unaffected by the things which the other stars suffer; for they are neither detained in their course nor do they stop, nor are they hindered so as to recede, nor indeed are they hidden by the light of the sun, as the other stars are. But being free and above all things, as faithful guardians and accurate overseers of the universe, they encompass the whole in the <term>Nycthemeron</term> <note>A Greek term for a full period of 24 hours, encompassing both a day and a night.</note> [or the space of night and day]. They also possess, with respect to us, the greatest power.” That is to say: “We say, O son, that the body [of the universe] is comprehensive of all things. Conceive, therefore, this to be as it were of a circular form.——But under the circle of this body the thirty-six decans are arranged, as the media of the whole circle of the zodiac.——These, likewise, must be understood to preside as guardians over every thing in the world, connecting and containing all things——and preserving the established order of all things ——Farther still, understand, O Tat, that these decans are impassive to the things which the other stars suffer. For neither being detained, do they stop their course, nor being impeded do they recede, nor are they, like the other stars, concealed as with a veil by the light of the sun. But being liberated above all things, they comprehend the universe as the guardians and accurate inspectors of it, in the <term>Nycthemeron</term> [or the space of night and day].——They also possess, with respect to us, the greatest power.”

P. 125. *So that what you add from Homer, “that the Gods are flexible,” it is not holy to assert.* The words of Homer are **even the gods themselves are flexible** <note>Original Greek: streptoi de te kai theoi autoi. This line suggests that the gods can be swayed by human prayer and sacrifice.</note>, and are to be found in *Iliad* ix. v. 493. <note>In modern editions of the Iliad, this quote is usually found at Book 9, line 497.</note> But when <term>Iamblichus</term> <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who sought to provide a philosophical defense for religious rituals and theurgy.</note> says, it is not holy to assert the Gods are flexible, he means that it is not holy according to the literal signification of the words; divine flexibility indicating nothing more than this, that those who through depravity were before unadapted to receive the illuminations of the Gods, and in consequence of this were subject to the power of avenging <term>dæmons</term> <note>In ancient philosophy, dæmons were intermediary spirits. Here, "avenging dæmons" refers to forces that execute natural justice or punishment upon the soul.</note>; when afterwards they obtain pardon of their guilt through prayers and sacrifices, and through methods of this kind apply a remedy to their vices, again become partakers of the goodness of the Gods. So that divine flexibility is a resumption of the participation of divine light and goodness by those who through inaptitude were before deprived of it.

<summary>This page describes the role of the thirty-six decans as eternal, unchanging guardians of the cosmic order and provides a Neoplatonic interpretation of Homer, arguing that "divine flexibility" refers to a change in the human soul's receptivity rather than a change in the Gods themselves.</summary>

P. 130. *Dæmons preside over the parts of our body.* <note>In ancient Greek philosophy, a "dæmon" (or daimon) is not an evil spirit, but a benevolent guardian or intermediary between the gods and the physical world.</note> Proclus in the fragments of his *Ten Doubts concerning Providence*, preserved by Fabricius in the eighth volume of his *Greek Library* <note>Original: "Bibliotheca Græca," a famous 18th-century bibliography of Greek literature.</note>, observes, “That the Gods, with an exempt transcendency, extend their providence to all things, but that dæmons, dividing their superessential subsistence, receive the guardianship of different herds of animals, distributing the providence of the Gods, as Plato says, as far as to the most ultimate division. Hence some of them preside over men, others over lions or other animals, and others over plants; and still more partially, some are the inspective guardians of the eye, others of the heart, and others of the liver.” He adds, “all things, however, are full of Gods, some of whom exert their <term>providential</term> <note>Providence refers to the divine care and foresight through which the universe is governed.</note> energies immediately, but others through dæmons as media: not that the Gods are incapable of being present to all things, but that ultimate are themselves unable to participate primary natures.” Hence it must be said that there is one principal dæmon, who is the guardian and governor of every thing that is in us, and many dæmons subordinate to him, who preside over our parts.

P. 134. *Hence it is requisite to consider how he may be liberated from these bonds.* “The one salvation of the soul herself,” says Proclus in his *Commentary on the Timaeus*, book 5, page 330, “which is extended by the <term>Demiurgus</term> <note>The "craftsman" or divine figure who fashioned the physical universe.</note>, and which liberates her from the circle of generation <note>The repetitive cycle of birth, death, and rebirth in the physical world.</note>, from abundant wanderings, and an inefficacious life, is her return to the <term>intellectual form</term> <note>The "intellectual" here refers to the realm of pure Mind or Intellect (Nous), which is the eternal home of the soul.</note>, and a flight from every thing which naturally adheres to us from generation. For it is necessary that the soul, which is hurled like seed into the realms of generation, should lay aside the stubble and bark, as it were, which she obtained from being disseminated into these fluctuating realms; and that purifying herself from every thing circumjacent, she should become an intellectual flower and fruit, delighting in an intellectual life, instead of <term>doxastic nutriment</term> <note>Based on the Greek word "doxa" (opinion); it refers to the "nourishment" of shifting beliefs and sensory appearances rather than stable truth.</note>, and pursuing the uniform and simple energy of the period of sameness, instead of the abundantly wandering motion of the period which is characterized by difference. For she contains each of these circles, and twofold powers. And of her horses one is good, but the other the contrary <note>A reference to Plato’s "Phaedrus," where the soul is compared to a charioteer driving two winged horses—one representing noble impulse and the other unruly desire.</note>. And one of these leads her to generation, but the other from generation to true being. The one also leads her round the <term>genesiurgic</term> <note>Relating to the world of "generation" or physical birth and material existence.</note>, but the other round the intellectual circle. For the period of the same and the similar elevates to intellect, and an intelligible nature, and to the

first and most excellent habit <note>In this context, "habit" (from the Greek *hexis*) refers to a stable state of being or a settled disposition of the soul.</note>. But this habit is that according to which the soul, being winged, governs the whole world, becoming assimilated to the Gods themselves. The middle of these, also, is the partially universal, when she lives in conjunction with her middle vehicle <note>The "vehicle" (*ochema*) is a Platonic concept of a "subtle body" or astral shell that carries the soul as it descends from the heavens into the physical body.</note>, as a citizen of generation <note>Generation refers to the physical world of change, birth, and decay, as opposed to the eternal realm of the divine.</note>. Their mysteries often focused on the soul's liberation from the cycle of reincarnation.</note> pray that they may obtain, together with the allotment of the [celestial] sphere, and a cessation of evil. 

But if the soul necessarily lives well when living according to the circle of sameness <note>A term from Plato’s *Timaeus* referring to the stable, eternal motion of the intellect, contrasted with the "circle of the different" or the wandering motion of the senses.</note>, much more must this be the case with divine souls. It is, however, possible for our soul to live according to the circle of sameness when purified, as Plato says. <term>Cathartic virtue</term> <note>From the Greek *katharsis* (purification). These are the virtues that cleanse the soul of material attachments.</note>, therefore, alone must be called the salvation of souls; since this cuts off, and vehemently obliterates, material natures, and the passions which adhere to her from generation; separates the soul and leads it to intellect, and causes it to leave on earth the vehicles with which she is invested. For how, without a medium, could they proceed into this body from immaterial spirits?

> "'The City of Dreadful Night' ranks with Omar Khayyam's *Rubaiyat* <note>original: "Rubai"</note> as a lyrical expression of despair, and it strikes a deeper note."—*Daily News* <note>original: "Daily Ne"</note>.
> "Thomson's work... has intensity, it has grip, it has that power of imaginative realism which gives to conceptions, embodied in words, the arresting quality of objects present to the senses... He was a creator and a singer, and in his creation and in his song his powers were finely co-ordinated <note>original: "co-ordina"</note> to imaginative ends. Even his most repellently pessimistic verse has the fascination of gloomy grandeur, and when, as in such poems as 'The Happy Poet' and 'Sunday up the River,' he rises into a wider atmosphere <note>original: "ampler ether"</note>, a divine air, his verse has not only the impressiveness of power, but the magic <note>original: "witchery"</note> of delight."—*Westminster Gazette*.
> "Messrs. Reeves & Turner and Mr. Dobell have published in two volumes <note>original: "volu"</note> the collected works of James Thomson, the poet of that 'melancholy <note>original: "melencolia"</note> which <note>original: "wh"</note> transcends all wit,' as he terms it himself. The sad story of his life is told with sympathy and fairness in a memoir by Mr. Bertram Dobell, who has edited the work. The pessimistic and unorthodox <note>original: "heterodox"</note> utterances of the author <note>original: "aut"</note> of 'The City of Dreadful Night' were never likely to be very popular, but this excellent edition will be very welcome to many who know the strength <note>original: "stren-"</note> and true poetry of many of his writings."—*Daily Telegraph*.
